speechtext: What was the date the last time the contract for carrying the mails from Alma station, Ont., on the Grand Trunk Railway, to the post office was advertised and let by public tender? To whom let and the amount? Has said contract been since renewed by the Postmaster General without tender? If so, to whom, and the remuneration paid for such services? What arrangement was made with the contractor when the service was increased?

Notices were issued on the 13th December, 1894, inviting tenders to be received at the department on the 25th January, 1895, for a contract for four years from the 1st April, 1895. Two tenders were received viz.:	From Alexander Gale, and Edward
O'Neill, each at fifteen cents per trip, and the tenderers having been asked to bid again, Mr. Gale, whose offer at twelve and a half cents per trip was the lowest, was awarded the contract at that rate, and a four years contract entered into with him. On the 11th June, 1895, the post office at Alma was removed, and the length of the route increased, and a corresponding increase was made in the rate of payment, which was made fourteen and a half cents per trip. It having been subsequently reported that the service had been satisfactorily performed, and the conditions advantageous to the public interest, and acting under the provisions of section 2, of clause 61, of the Postal Act, authority was given for the renewal of Mr. Gale's contract for a further term of four years from the 1st of April, 1901, on the same terms and conditions. On the 1st of August, 1899, the service of Alma was increased from two to four trips daily, and a temporary agreement was made with Mr. Gale for the additional semi-daily service at thirty-five dollars per annum. This agreement to continue until the expiration of the existing contract viz.: March 31, 1903.

DAYIS (Saskatchewan) moved ;
That this House is of opinion that the public interests demand that the railway companies of Canada should at the earliest moment be brought under control of a board of railway commissioners, clothed with full power to enforce the provisions of the Railway Act, and to prescribe and enforce the observance of such regulations as may be necessary in the public interest.
He said :	Mr. Speaker, the motion I
place in your hands is not new to this House. It was first introduced by the late member for Winnipeg, Mr. Jamieson, and later by the late member for Macdonald, Mr. Rutherford, in 1899. Last year I had the honour of moving practically the same resolution in this House with reference to the appointment of a railway commission. Those who are interested in this question

liad reason to hope that the government would take some action last year toward the establishment of a railway commission for the purpose of controlling the railroads In this country, and settling disputes between the people and those corporations. But the government have not done so, and still there is a growing feeling in this country that something of that kind should be done. We know as a matter of fact that all agitation in this country with reference to government ownership and control of railroads is the outcome of the way the railroads have been oppressing the people, and discriminating against one part of the country in favour of another. When we turn to the province of Manitoba and see what is taking place there to-day, when we find that the people of that province, in their desire to get relief from railroad monopoly, have undertaken practically to purchase 350 odd miles of railway for seven million dollars, a railroad which is not worth more than three and a half million dollars, we must come >to the conclusion that the people are in earnest in their determination to get relief from the monopolies under which they are labouring.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this sentiment is growing stronger in the country day by day. We see articles in the newspapers and read of speeches made on public platforms in favour of government control of railroads.
1 may say that I am in favour of government control. But the kind of control' government should have over railroads is a matter on which there is a great difference of opinion in this country. Some hon. gentlemen in this House are of opinion that the government should undertake the purchase or lease of all the railroads in this country. In that opinion I cannot concur, for the simple reason that I think that would be too large an obligation for the people of this country to undertake at. the present time ; nor do I think it is necessary for the government to purchase or lease all the railroads in this country. We heard a statement the other day by an hon. gentleman in this House that we could lease the Canadian Pacific Railway system and also the Grand Trunk Railway system for $1 a year each. Well, Mr. Speaker, taking the same basis of calculation as was adopted in Manitoba, I suppose the hon. gentleman would expect the people of this country to assume all the liabilities of these railroads, and all railroads that we might rent in this country. Now, when we take into consideration that the majority of the railroads in this coutnry are bonded for double what they are worth, I do not think this proposition will commend itself to the people of this country. Take the case of the Calgary and Edmonton road as one in point. There is a road bonded for five million dollars ; and I think you will find the statement in the report of the Minister
of Railways that the road did not cost more than three million dollars. I wonder if those hon. gentlemen who propose that we should lease these roads or purchase them, think we should pay to any corporation five million dollars for a road that they tell us only cost three million dollars. Take the Regina and Long Lake road, and you will find the same thing occurs there. You will find the statement in the report of the Minister of Railways that that road cost something like two and a half million dollars, and you will find that it is bonded for $3,800,000 ; and so on all along the line.
I suppose there is hardly a road in this country that is not bonded for double what the road is worth. In my humble judgment, it would be a very foolish thing for the government to go into a scheme of this kind, but, there is another system of controlling the roads. We have power by the Railway Act, under section 224 and some other sections, to regulate rates and see that there is no discrimination. This is all the control the people want. All that we require is to provide some machinery to make that provision effective. It may be said that we have the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, but the Railway Committee of the Privy Council is composed of men who are very busy, who have not time to take up all the cases that should come before them, and the business of the country is rapidly increasing. The carrying corporations are extending the lines of transportation, opening up new roads, and it is time that we had some authority that we could rely upon to bring the railways under control, and to do away with unjust discriminations. Now, I do not think the people of the country care very much whether the Canadian Pacific Railway, or the Grand Trunk Railway, or any other companies own the railways, or whether they operate them, [DOT] so long as the roads are under proper control, and so long as they are not oppressed by being charged excessive rates for carrying the products of the country from one part to the other. We have paid millions of dollars in subsidies to railway corporations in aid of the railways that have been built during the last few years, and not only have we paid millions of dollars in money, but we have given some sixty odd million acres of the best and most fertile lands in the North-west Territories to railway corporations, and I think it is not an unreasonable request to be made by the people, who really have the greatest interest in the soil of the west, that somebody should be appointed to control railway corporations and to see that the people are afforded a reasonable amount of relief.
