speechtext: Yes ; they were to hold office during good behaviour, one of the commissioners being a business man, another a railway man, and another a lawyer. So that you see that they appointed a railway commission years and years ago in Great Britain in the same way that we are asking to have a commission appointed in this country. In the United States, and we will be more interested, I suppose, because that country is close at hand and we know what is taking place there, nearly all the states of the union have had railway commissions. I have here, in my hand, the 23rd annual report of the Iowa State Railway Commission, and if any hon. gentleman will take the trouble to read this report, he will come to the conclusion that

the sooner we have a railway commission in this country the better it will be for all concerned, not only for the people, but for the railway corporations themselves, because, I suppose, there are cases where people complain without having justification for the complaints they make. We find that this is no new or radical proposal. In the United States they have two kinds of railway commissions ; in the old states, Massachusetts, for instance, they have what is called an advisory commission. An advisory commission is a commission which is appointed without power to arrange rates or settle disputes. They are appointed to arbitrate and advise as to disputes, and to make a report to the legislature, if a settlement has not been made, so that the legislature will then be in a position to legislate intelligently, and give relief to the people. In the western states they take a more advanced view ; Illinois led off, and the other states followed in the appointment of commissions with power to regulate freight rates, to settle disputes and to deal with complaints of discrimination, not only that, but to deal with any dispute that may arise between the individual and the railway corporation. I have here the report of the Iowa commission, showing in one case where they have settled a dispute between a railway corporation and grain shippers about the scarcity of cars. That is a thing that we are troubled with all the time in the North-west Territories. Again, there is a case of excessive rates charged which the commission settled. Again, the people complained that they were not getting sufficient facilities for the shipping and handling of grain, and this case was settled. There are two cases in which complaints were made by shippers that they were overcharged. These cases were settled. Another case involving the laying of a side track into an elevator was settled. We have, in the west, disputes as to getting side tracks laid in to elevators. There are several other cases besides those which I have mentioned which were settled in Iowa. Any person reading this report must come to the conclusion that such a commission as this would be a good thing for us to have in this country. In reference to a commission here, I would suggest it should be established on the same lines as those adopted in the western states, a commission with power to deal with all disputes between the individual and the railway corporation. Another thing I would suggest in reference to the functions of a railway commission in this country, is this : There is not the least doubt, as every hon. gentleman in this House knows, that a great deal of the time of the House, not only this year, but in years gone by, has been taken up in dealing with what are called ' straw charters.' Charter-mongers come here to get charters in the hope of being able to secure a subsidy. The

moment they have a charter and get the subsidy they have something to sell which has not cost them anything. They toil not, neither do they spin. It is high time that that sort of thing should be stopped, and that these charter-mongers should be choked off.
If we had a proper railway commission appointed we should have all applications for railway charters submitted to that commission, which would investigate at to whether there was necessity for the proposed roads being constructed, and on the report of the railway commission for or against, parliament could deal with the application intelligently. That railway commission could also report on the probable cost of the construction of the road, and then parliament could insert a clause empowering the incorporators to bond that road only for what it was likely to cost, so we would not have a repetition of the scandals in connection with the Calgary and Edmonton road and the Regina and Long Lake road in which people were enticed-to use a mild expression-to invest their money without any chance of getting it back. That was an injury to the credit of Canada. If all these applications for charters were referred to a competent commission we would have fewer applications here session after session. There are cases too in which legitimate railway companies ask for charters which should not be granted, because if you build a line parallel to an existing line the work will have to be divided between the competing lines, and somebody will have to pay the piper. If a line is paralleled in one portion of the country the people living on that line in another portion of the country will have to make up for the loss, and in days gone by the people of the North-west Territories and Manitoba have suffered in that respect. We feel strongly on this railway question in Manitoba and the Territories, and we have a right to do so because we have suffered for years and years from railway oppression and extortion. Nevertheless you have gentlemen, employed no doubt by railway corporations, travelling through the country and writing letters to the press trying to make people believe that there is no discrimination and that the people in one part of the country are treated just the same as the people in another part. In the North-west Territories we are some 2,000 miles from the head of ocean navigation at Montreal and close to 3,000 miles from the sea-board. The great problem with our people is as to how they are to get their products to the markets of the world so as to enable them to compete with people living in other localities. We do not expect to get our produce carried for nothing ; all we want is reasonable rates. We are prepared to pay just as much as they pay in any other portion of the Dominion, but when we are made to pay
double it is time for us to raise our voices against this oppression.
I have taken the trouble to prepare a few figures in connection with this discrimination. It has been said there is no discrimination in 'the west, but I am prepared to prove to the House and to the country that discrimination does exist there in connection with the carrying of our products. Look at the enormous freight rates we pay on wheat alone. We pay 14 cents per hundred pounds for carrying our wheat from the city of Winnipeg to Fort William or Port Arthur, a distance of 448 miles.
It was 21 cents a few years ago.

Yes, that is true. Up to three years ago it was 17 cents a hundred pounds from Winnipeg to Port Arthur, and then the government of the day came to the relief of the settlers in that portion of the country, and in the arrangement they made for the building of the Crow's Nest Pass railway they got a reduction of 3 cents a hundred pounds on the freight rate. Let me tell the House that that comparatively small reduction, on the average wheat crop of the province of Manitoba amounted to something like $600,000 saved to the farmers. The production of wheat in that country is increasing by leaps and bounds and we may assume that if this increase continues, then in five years about one million dollars would be saved to the farmers of that country on account of this small reduction alone.
What distance did you say that wheat was hauled 7

About 448 miles. If we take into consideration that wheat is hauled by the Canada Atlantic and Parry Sound Railway, including water stretches from Chicago to Montreal for 4J cents a bushel, while we in the North-west have to pay 8f cents a bushel from Winnipeg to Fort William ; it ' will be seen that it was high time that the * people of Manitoba loaded themselves with ' liabilities to the extent of some $14,000,000 | in order to try and get relief.

cents a bushel for liauling it 448 miles. We liave been told that there is no discrimination in the west, but I have gone to the trouble to get the present western local tariff as well as the traders' tariff, and also the general tariff, because these gentlemen have two or three tariffs in the west ; they have a tariff for traders, and a tariff for the ordinary individual, and I cannot understand why one person wishing to ship a car-load of goods should be called upon to pay more because he is not a jobber.
Do you mean car-load and part car-load lots.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Car-load lots.
Have they two distinctive tariffs by car-loads ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
They have two tariffs, one for the trader and another for the other man. Some goods are classified as No. 2 by local rate which are the same as No. 5 in carloads.
From Toronto to Winnipeg, a distance of 1,091 miles, groceries and goods of that kind, which are fifth class freight, pay 82 cents per hundred pounds, while from Winnipeg to Prince Albert, a distance of 609 miles, the rate for fifth class freight is 80 cents per hundred pounds. We pay in the west, within two cents a hundred pounds to carry goods 609 miles, of what the Toronto people pay to haul their goods 1,091 miles. Let us look at the condition of affairs on the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I am well aware that the government have not the same control over the Canadian Pacific Railway on the main line as they have on the branch lines, but it appears to me that the Canadian Pacific Railway management are charging these exorbitant rates to a greater extent on the branch lines where the government might be expected to step in and give the people relief. On the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway from Winnipeg to Calgary, a distance of 840 miles, the first class freight rate is 81.82 per hundred pounds and the second class, $1.57.
Is that by car-loads or by smaller quantities ?
It is according to the way you send it, by car-loads or not. Fifth class would not be fifth class if sent at local rates. It is the ordinary rate for car-loads at local rates.
That is in small quantities.
That does not make any difference for the purpose of my present argument. I am showing that on" the same class of goods and the same quantities sent

to different points, they sometimes charge more for the shorter distance than they do for the longer distance. From Winnipeg to Calgary, a distance of 840 miles,' the first-class rate is $1.82 per hundred pounds ; second class, $1.57 ; third class, $1.25 ; fourth class, 90 cents ; fifth class, 80 cents. Now, take the rate from Winnipeg to Prince Albert, a distance of 609 miles, according to the Canadian Pacific Railway folder, or some 230 miles less than the distance from Winnipeg to Calgary. The rates are : first class, $1.89, or 7 cents per hundred pounds more than from Winnipeg to Calgary : second class, $1.57, the same as to Calgary ; third class, $1.25 ; fourth class, 90 cents ; fifth class, 80 cents. I would have no objection if they charged the people of Calgary just as much as they charge the people of Prince Albert ; but wThen they charge the people of Prince Albei't 7 cents per hundred pounds more than the people of Calgary, though the distance is shorter by 2.30 miles, I think the people of Prince Albeit have good reason to kick.
Take lumber. The rate from British Columbia to all points in the Territories is 50 cents per hundred pounds. From British Columbia to Regina, from British Columbia to Prince Albert, or from British Columbia to Winnipeg, the rate is the same-50 cents per hundred pounds. I have been told on good authority by a gentleman in the business, that occasionally they send it to Fort William, 800 miles further on than Winnipeg, at the same rate. What position does that place the people of my district in ? It kills our local trade. We have three sawmills in Prince Albert, and if they want to ship lumber out they have to pay prohibitory rates, so that it is impossible for them to compete. I do not think that is a fair way to treat our people.
I have made a comparison of the maximum tariff on first-class goods west of Lake Superior with the maximum tariff of the Canada Atlantic Railway on first-class goods. The rate in the west for 30 miles is 27 cents, on 50 miles 35 cents, on 100 miles 54 cents, on 200 miles 80 cents, on 250 miles 92 cents, and on 450 miles $1.33 per hundred pounds. Compare these rates with what the people in eastern Canada have to pay. Between Ottawa and Depot Harbour, the maximum tariff rate on the Canada Atlantic, for 56 miles is 26 cents, for 102 miles 34 cents, for 200 miles 46 cents, for 254 miles 46 cents, as against 92 cents in Manitoba and the Territories for 250 miles. For 363 miles on the Canada Atlantic, the rate is also for 46 cents per hundred pounds.
We hear a great deal about the railroad monopolies of the United States. Gentlemen connected with the Canadian Pacific Railway try to make the people of this country believe that if the large railroad corporations of the United States got a footing in this country, our people would be bound

to suffer. It is all a question of sentiment. We know that the people of the United States are getting their work done by the railways for one-half of what the people of this country have to pay the Canadian Pacific Railway for the same work. These are the maximum tariff rates in the state of Iowa, fixed by commission : 30 miles, 17 T6 cents per hundred pounds ; 50 miles, 20 cents, as against 35 cents charged by the Canadian Pacific Railway in the west ; 100 miles, 24 cents, as against 54 cents in the west ; 200 miles 40 cents, as against 80 cents in the west ; 450 miles, 634 cents, as against $1.33 charged by the Canadian Pacific Railway in the west for performing the same service. And still we are told by those gentlemen who want to exclude competition from this country, that if we allow the American railroads to get a footing here, the country will be ruined. I hope to see the day when some of these American railroad corporations will get a footing in the country, so that we may get relief from these excessive charges, and that magnificent country west of Lake Superior may get a chance to develop. I do not see why the Canadian Pacific Railway corporation should own that country. Is it not enough that the people of this country gave that corporation $110,000,000 in lands and money, but we must hand over the whole country to them ? I hope the members of this House will see to it that when other companies seek for charters to build railways into that country, those charters shall be granted, notwithstanding what the Canadian Pacific Railway Company may say.
I have another statement which has been sent to me by the president of the Board of Trade of Prince Albert, Mr. F. O. Baker. He says the rate from Winnipeg to Prince Albert. 003 miles, on first-class goods, is $1.89, while the rate from Winnipeg to Regina, 356 miles on the main line, is $1.12, while on the branch line from Regina to Prince Albert, for 247 miles, we have to pay $1.15. In other words, we pay 3 cents more for 250 miles than the people of Regina pay for 356 miles. That is a clear case of discrimination against the town in which I live.
We have heard a great deal about the long haul, and I wish to draw the attention of the House to that phase of the question. Let us look at the rates on coal oil, which is a commodity not used so much in the towns and villages as by the farming population. From Petrolia to Winnipeg, a distance of 1,200 miles, the fifth-class rate is 61| cents per hundred pounds. From Winnipeg to Prince Albert, 609 miles, the rate is 65 cents. So that we are paying 31 cents more for hauling our coal oil 609 miles than is paid for sending it 1.200 miles. There is a case of discrimination. It might be supposed that you would get a lower rate from Petrolia to Prince Albert because of the long haul. But if you add the two
local rates together, from Petrolia to Winnipeg, and from Winnipeg to Prince Albert, they come to $1,261, whereas the through rate from Petrolia to Prince Albert is $1,374. or 11 cents more. In other words, you could take a car-load of coal oil from Petrolia to Winnipeg, unload it there, load it again on the cars and ship it through to Prince Albert, and you would save 11 cents per hundred pounds. And yet, we are told that the people of Prince Albert have no discrimination to complain of.
I have taken this from the Toronto Globe, and I believe it to be true. It certainly has never been contradicted. From Brantford, Eng., to Toronto, the rate on wool is 17 cents per 100 pounds. Compare this with the rate from Crane Lake, N.W.T., to Toronto of $1.50 per 100 pounds, and the excessive charge imposed on the people of the North-west Territories is at once apparent. How is it possible for the people of that country to live and pay such exorbitant freight rates ?
Take the rates on cattle, the largest industry in the North-west Territories, and a very large one in Manitoba. From Prince Albert to Montreal the rate is $180 per car. and the value of a car-load of cattle is $680. I am not grumbling at this, but want to make a comparison. The rate from Toronto to Prince Albert on a car-load of apples, the average value of which is $190, is something like $375 now, and two or three years ago it was $518. I paid $518 freight on a car-load of apples from Seaforth to Prince Albert. When I ordered the apples. I had no idea that I would be charged such an exorbitant rate.
How much did you pay for the apples 7

$190, and I paid $518 freight. As a consequence, I lost about $250 on the car-load, and I did not go into the apple business any more. This is a matter which affects, not only the people of the Territories and Manitoba, but of the eastern provinces as well. When you have good crops of apples in the eastern provinces, you find it difficrdt to dispose of them, and they are often left to rot on the ground. But if reasonable freight rates were charged, you could easily dispose of them in the Territories and Manitoba. AVe produce wheat and cattle, but we cannot produce fruit, and are willing to exchange. But if a man has to pay $5 a barrel freight on apples, you can easily see that the average farmer cannot afford to indulge in luxuries of that kind in order to enable the Canadian Pacific Railway to pay its president $50,000 a year and the rest of the officials in proportion
In the early history of the country we expected to have to pay rather high freight rates, but it is high time these rates should be reduced. We hear a great deal about

American railways coming in to oppress our people. Let me show what the people of Massachusetts have to pay for hauling freight per ton over their railways and show you how these rates were reduced from year to year. The following statement gives the freight and passenger rates :

In the Territories we pay three cents and four cents passenger rates per mile, and up to last year we paid five cents per mile on the Regina Long Lake and Saskatchewan Road, yet this country has paid that road three times more than it has cost. We gave
it 6,400 acres of the finest lands in the coun- ___________ „„vv.rai3J.UI allll
try per mile. They will not take ordinary | we had a commission appointed to wipe out Mr. DAVIS.
land, and I understand there is a suit pending because they refuse to take the lands offered and want the choicest. Besides 6,400 acres per mile, they get $80,000 per year for twenty years for carrying the mails, and they have never earned more than $2,000 or $3,000 a year in that service. Take the lands at $3 an acre-and they have not sold one acre at less, and some they have sold as high as $6 or $7 an acre-that makes $19,200 per mile as the value of the land, taking its lowest value of $3 per acre. Then take the cash subsidy of $80,000 a year for twenty years, and you will see that this corporation has received not less than $20,000 per mile.
I have seen an estimate which figures out that the $80,000 per mile for twenty years capitalized is equal to $6,000 per mile.

I am making a very low estimate. The value of the lands is $19,200, and the bon. member for Lisgar tells us that the value of the mail subsidy is $6,000 per mile, which would bring the total subsidy up to $25,000 per mile. What did the road cost ? Take the report of its cost issued by the company, and you can rest assured that when they made that report they made it so as to show as large a cost as possible. It shows that the road cost $10,000 a mile, and the people have given them actually $20,000 a mile. I suppose their heavy charges for freight and passengers are to meet the interest on the bonds, and it appears they have bonded the road for $3,800,000, although it only cost them $2,500,000. Into whose pockets the difference went I do not know, but I do not think it is fair that we should be called on to pay the interest on money that did not go into the construction of the road at all, but into the pockets of the speculators.
In 1895, the last year for which I have a return, the people of the state of Massachusetts only had to pay 1-78 cents per mile passenger rate, and yet we are told by interested parties that if you allow American railways and capital to come into Canada our people will be oppressed. For my part I would like to see more competition, and hope the day will come when we will have it.
It is high time the government took some action with reference to this commission. There is an agitation for the establishment of a railway commission going on in the country and gathering force as it goes. All the leading papers in the country are taking this question up, and it is one the government cannot ignore. They will have to take some action and take it in the near future. Let them appoint a board of railway commissioners for only four or five years if you like. Such commissions have been working in the United States for twenty-five or thirty years and have proved successful, and if

the discrimination and force the railway corporations to impose fair and moderate charges, as we have the power to do under the Railway Act, you would soon find the cry for government ownership and control of railways disappearing. All this agitation for government ownership is due to the fact that the people are desirous that something should be done to relieve them of the oppressive railways rates which are now charged.

Before that motion is put, I would like to offer one or two observations. I may say that after a study of the railway question carefully for the last four or five years, I am scarcely so sanguine as my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), that the appointment of a railway commission would accomplish all that he thinks it would. I will tell you why I think so. In the first place, the railways have been stocked and bonded for an amount far in excess of their cost, in many cases double and treble the cost of the roads. Now, they always maintain that before you should allow government to regulate the rates on railroads, you must allow interest to be earned on all the stock and on all the bonds that the road carries. They will meet you with this proposition, that there are vested interests, that capitalists in Europe have purchased these bonds and this stock in good faith, and that it is only reasonable to allow a proper interest to be earned on this stock and bonds. There is another reason why I think a railway commission would be largely ineffective. When the contract for the Canadian Pacific Railway was made in 1881, exactly twenty years ago on the 15th of last month, a provision was inserted whereby the company was allowed to earn 10 per cent on the capital actually invested in the road before the government could exercise any control of the rates. That is a statutory provision which would meet the commission at once. If this railway commission were appointed it would be absolutely unable to control the rates on the Canadian Pacific Railway until they have earned 10 per cent on the capital actually invested.
So here is one difficulty that would meet you, the determination of the amount of capital that was invested in that enterprise. Now, in order to get over that difficulty I moved a resolution in this House some four sessions ago for the appointment of a commission by parliament to ascertain the actual cost of the Canadian Pacific Railway in order that parliament, if it desired to secure control of the rates, might know when the company earned 10 per cent on the money actually invested. My own recollection is that the gross earnings of the Canadian Pacific Raiway run up to nearly thirty million dollars, and that the actual
earnings to-day are a good deal more than 10 per cent, probably thirty per cent, I do not know but 100 per cent on anything they have put in. I wish the House clearly to understand this proposition. Why should the Canadian Pacific Railway be allowed to earn 10 per cent, or any per cent whatever, on capital that the Canadian people have put into the enterprise ? As the hon. member for Saskatchewan pointed out. although he did not give you all the facts, the Canadian people gave to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company twenty-five million dollars in cash, and it handed over completed railroads, the Thunder Bay branch, the Yale and Cariboo section, and a section in eastern Canada, all of which had cost the Canadian people thirty-five million dollars. That is to say, the government made practically a cash payment to that company of sixty million dollars. In addition to that, we gave them twenty-five million acres of the best lands in that vast country ; and so particular is this company with regard to the selection of these lands that the Minister of the Interior told us the other day they have declined to accept all their land grant because they are very anxious to obtain the very best land in that country. What is the result ? The member for Saskatchewan told us a moment ago that the land grants on the Regina and Long Lake Railway have brought $3, $4 and $5 an acre, they have never sold an acre for less. I was able to show on the floor of parliament last session that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company never sold an acre of land, in Manitoba, at least, for less than an average of $4 or $5 an acre. But let us take the land grant at $3 an acre, and we find that in addition to giving that company sixty million dollars in cash practically, we gave them seventy-five million dollars worth of land, or a total subsidy to that company of practically $135,000,000. not speaking of all the other concessions that we have given them.
Mr. Speaker, let me state that the Canadian Pacific Railway syndicate's own estimate of the whole cost of construction of that railway was $91,500,000, and that included $10,000,000 for equipment. Now, having given the company something in the neighbourhood of forty-three million dollars more than the actual cost of the road, why should we be called upon to stick to that clause allowing them to earn 5 per cent on what it actually cost ? Why should the country be obliged to pay, in high freight rates, 10 per cent on the money that the country actually gave to the company ? My contention in parliament four or five years ago was that we should appoint a commission to ascertain if that company spent $1 of its own money in the construction of that road; and If that company did not spend $1, then,

haying ascertained that fact, we would he able to say :	You shall not be allowed to
earn 10 per cent on what the country gave you, and we shall take control of your rates. If parliament would adopt the suggestion I made a few years ago for the appointment of that commission to ascertain exactly what the company had put into the enterprise, then I think we would be able to control the rates on this vast transcontinental road. I maintain that until you are able to control the rates on the Canadian Pacific Railway, your railway commission is in a large measure bound to be ineffective.
The only cure for the transportation question that I can see, is in government ownership and control of railroads. But I do not think at the present time that the finances of this country, would warrant the government in purchasing all the railroad systems of this country. I believe that the government should do what I urged on the floor of parliament two sessions ago. The government now own the Intercolonial Railway, which they have recently extended into Montreal, and I believe if it could secure control of the Parry Sound Railroad, and then acquire control of the Rainy River Railway, and get access into those vast wheat fields of the west, we could effectively control the transportation question of this country, and it would not cost a large amount either. It would not require a great deal to control the Parry Sound road up to Parry Sound, and afterwards securing railway communication from the head of lake navigation into the wheat fields of the west, then the question would be largely solved. If the people of that great country are able to send their products away at decent rates, then I do not think there will be much to complain of. If the government controls one road and is able to fix the rate, then all other roads would be obliged to meet the rates which the government makes on its road.
When the question was before parliament two sessions ago, when these vast subsidies were given to the Rainy River Railway,
I myself, seconded by the member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) moved a number of resolutions relating to that subject. I wished to have the government appoint an officer who should superintend the construction of that railroad, in order that we might ascertain exactly what it cost-so that, if parliament desired, at any later date, to put into effect the government ownership of even one railway, it would be able to acquire this road with the knowledge of the actual cost. And I added in the resolution that it should be acquired at the cost price, less the subsidies which the country had given to the road. That resolution, I am sorry to say, did not carry. I believe that one reason why it did not carry was Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
that the House was not fully seized of the importance of the question. I believe that lion, members had not given sufficient study to the transportation question, and did not understand the true nature of the proposition I put forward at that time. I moved another resolution-and I think there are signs throughout the country that the people are beginning to understand the importance of the question-that the rates on that road should never be higher than would produce 6 per cent on the cost. The crux of the transportation question is the limiting of capitalization. You must not allow charges, fixed or otherwise, to appear in these enterprises more than is actually necessary. If you limit the stocking and bonding to the actual necessities of the case, it is easy to see how you protect the producer, for you can then control the rates; you will not be obliged to allow charges to pay a percentage of 4, 6 or 10 per cent on capital that never went into the road. What has happened in regard to the Rainy River-road on which we made such a strong fight ? In addition to the $4,000 per mile which the legislature of Ontario granted to that enterprise, in addition to the $0,400 in cash that this parliament granted, making-in all $10,400 a mile given by the public to assist that road, we find that we also gave power to stock this road for $28,000 a mile, and to bond it for $20,000 a mile. So that, for all time, that road is loaded with a capitalization of $48,000 per mile, and for all time the settlers will oe obliged to pay the interest in freight rates on that enormous capitalization. And what are we told here to-day ? We are told that the Manitoba government is coming to the relief of this company by guaranteeing the bonds of the road for $20,000 a mile. What would be the result ?
Does that include the whole mileage ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Two hundred and ninety miles.
It does not cover any portion of the mileage of the Rainy River Railway, does it ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It covers the mileage, the hon. minister will understand. from the western terminus of the Port Arthur, Duluth and Western, a point known as Stanley station. The company that own that through road bought the Port Arthur, Duluth and Western. It goes two hundred and ninety miles west to Fort Frances, and the province of Manitoba, judging from the reports, is about to guarantee the bonds on that section for $20,000 a mile.
Is any portion of that in Ontario ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It is all in Ontario. The point I make, the hon. minister apprehends, is that the country gave $10,400 a mile in cash, and the people also will give this 4 per cent guarantee on $20,000 a mile, so that the people will have practically given in cash and undertaken to give in a guarantee, as good as cash, $30,400 a mile. And, as I tell you, the result is that for all time the people of that country are obliged to pay high freight rates on this over-capitalization. I believe the time has come when there are sufficient people in this country who understand this question to say that unless we limit the stocking and bonding to the actual necessities of the road we shall never be able to exercise any effective control over freight rates. I have reason to believe that a strong attempt will be made this session to limit the stocking and bonding of railway lines in order that a commission such as my hon. friend (Mr. Davis) moves for may be of some effect.
Now, I am not prepared to say that a railway commission such as is called for in the motion would not be of considerable advantage. Probably, in doing away with discrimination, in regulating long hauls and short hauls, in regulating rates over branch and trunk lines, it might be of some effect. I believe, and I think it likely the hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) agrees with me, with the 10 per cent clause as it is, and with the lines over-capitalized as they are, even with a railway commission, we shall not be able to exei'cise any effective control. Why, Sir, let me give two or three facts with regard to what this country has given for its railway system. The people of Canada have given in cash, up to the present time-and I include the municipalities, the provincial-governments and the Dominion government -$223,000,000 in cash for railways. From what the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) told us the other day, it appears that the country has contributed 60,000,000 acres of land for the construction of railways. You will agree with me that, in view of the statements made by my hon. friend (Mr. Davis), and in view of the facts produced in this House from time to time, $3 an acre is a very moderate estimate of the value of this land. Estimating on that basis, you will find that the people of this country have given $403,000,000 for the construction of railways. Just let the hon. members of this House pause and think for a moment what that means. It means that the people have given far more than would build the entire system of railways in this country. And what do we own ? We own the Intercolonial Railway, which, I presume, actually cost about $25,000,000-we paid $50,000,000 for it, but it was not worth that 27
amount of money. Think of this expenditure in connection with the proposition that we shall attempt to regulate rates by appointing a commission. We cannot do it. The only way in which rates can be effectively controlled in this country is for the government to own and control one road on which there shall be no over-capitalization, and on which fair rates shall be charged, based on the actual cost of the road. When the government takes that position, I assert, we shall have the transportation question effectively solved. As I have said, I am not one who says that the country should, at present, go into the enterprise of controlling all the railroads of the country. But, I would be willing to go even that far, if we cannot get justice in any other way. Look at the example of the Australasian colonies. According to an article in the North American Review that I read recently these colonies have paid $600,000,000 for their railways. At present those railways charge more favourable rates than ours do, rates in accordance with the condition of the settlers, and they are able to pay 3 per cent on that vast sum of money, and pay operating expenses as well. If that can be done in the Australasian colonies, why can it not be done in Canada ? It is perfectly true that we have made this bad start; it is perfectly true that we have paid this vast sum of money and have practically no return for it. But, surely, Sir, we are not going to perpetuate this colossal error. The time has come when the transportation question is knocking at the door of parliament, and unless the people's representatives deal with this question, I want to say the people will deal with their representatives later on. I shall not oppose the motion, Mr. Speaker, because, as I said, I believe some good may come of the regulation of these rates in various ways. I shall listen with great interest to any debate that may occur on this question, and particularly to the views which the government may give us at the present time. I may say, before I sit down, that I think if anything is to be done in this matter it ought to be done soon. We have been led to expect from session to session that we would have this railway commission appointed, and I think it would be gratifying to members of this House, and also to the country, to know that the question was soon to be settled one way or the other and not keep it dangling before the public any longer.

Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of offering any remarks upon this question until I heard of the deplorable state of Canada in a railway sense from the two hon. gentlemen who have been discussing it. I have got up to say that I feel quite differently about it. I cannot see any reason why such a pessimistic view should be taken of our present



transportation facilities and of the position of Canada in regard to its railways and to the transportation question. I did not suppose that on this motion we would be going into the whole railway and transportation question, because the question involved in the motion is only one of the very important propositions in connection with our | railway transportation system. I am at a loss to understand the cause of the grievous state of affairs that these hon. gentlemen seem to have discovered in regard to our railways, not that I am interested any more than they are in railways. Since I have been in this House I have had no interest in railways ; I have none to-day any more than they have. I have had some experience of the difficulties of getting railways built in this country, because the only railways that I have been interested in were roads of a local character where we wanted to build them through to different parts of the province of Ontario, some years ago and some very recently. We had very great difficulty in accomplishing this. How did we manage to get them ? Something like the manner in which the Canadian Pacific Railway was got. The most of them were of a much smaller pattern. We wanted to get railways through the old-settled parts of the country where the pioneers had gone in years ago with their axes and yoke of oxen and hewed out their homes. These pioneers had for fifty or seventy-five years been taxed for carrying on all the public affairs of the country. We found it impossible to get these roads constructed except upon the principle of the people helping themselves. The people offered bonuses. There is scarcely a township between Lake Erie and Georgian Bay that has not contributed by bonus to obtain railways. Why ? Hid they do it to give away their money ? Did they do it on any other principle than a mere business proposition ?
It was a business proposition. You can be sure that the hardy pioneers who built up the country, and who were a long time without transportation facilities, having discovered that railways would be a great boon to them, would not have given away their hard-earned dollars unless they thought I there would be some return. Why did they give away anything ? Because it was found impossible to get money to build railways [DOT]otherwise. So they offered what are known as bonuses and the government of Ontario, before the Dominion government entertained the proposition at all, established a system of giving bonuses to railways, municipalities following that up. But, money in addition to the bonuses was required, and I have had considerable experience in helping to secure the construction of railways in that part of the country, not, however, in the way of making money out of them.
I happened to be one of those gentlemen who did not have much money to put into such enterprises, but who tried to find Mr. TISDALE.
means of raising, with the assistance of the municipalities and the government, the balance of the money required. The government and the municipalities knew that they were giving this money to enable the balance of the money to be obtained which was always a hard proposition. These hon. gentlemen who have spoken say that it was very unwise and that great difficulties have resulted. I totally disagree with them when they say that it makes a great deal of difference how much stock or bonds are issued. It did not make scarcely any difference for the reason that the propositions in those days were left largely to the promoters. We did not care so much whether the promoters got permission to issue a lot of bonds or a few bonds, a large amount of stock or a small amount. We were satisfied whichever way they could work the scheme as long as we got the road after having subscribed our money as taxpayers. Go through the country to-day, even through Manitoba and the North-west Territories, where there is so much talk about the Canadian Pacific Railway, and ask the people there if they would have these railways taken away from them and get their money back. They would laugh at you and very properly. I want to go roughly and quickly over this question. Apart altogether from what has been given by the country or for what railways have been bonded, the money that has been put into railways in Canada in addition has never returned \\ per cent to the people who put it up. That is a proposition which, if hon. gentlemen will look into it, will be borne out. Take the Grand Trunk Railway, for instance, the road most heavily loaded with bonds, stock and preferences. Why was it so ? Why did we from time to time help it ? Because, if the government of Canada, in times past, had not come forward and given assistance it would have entirely disappeared. Millions of money had been sent across the sea for investment in the road, and widows and orphans had put their money into it in the belief that they were going to get a big return. I remember once in the history of the road that .$10,000,000 of common stock was sold at 10 per cent or ten cents on the dollar and the company induced people to believe that they would get big returns that they bought it. If it had not been for that financial transaction, away back in the history of the road, the Grand Trunk Railway would have been forced to shut up. That was the pioneer road in Ontario and Quebec.
I remember how glad I was to see it. 1 had never seen a railway train and I had never seen any cars, except a few on the old Northern Railway which ran out of Toronto. That stock is worth less to-day, about five or six cents on the dollar, than half a century ago when these people bought it. The government had to help the company out of a hole with several millions of dollars.

Take the actual money which has been put into the road and there are many millions upon which not one cent of return in interest has been obtained. The bonded debt and stock were so large, looking at it in this day, that it would be absurd to try and float a scheme of that kind now. But it cost the government of Canada a good deal. That was the pioneer road and there are thousands of people across the sea, or their descendants, who will never receive a cent of return on their investment. It is well that we should look upon the other side of the picture. I am one of those who believe that the first business is to get the railway, secondly, to get it on the best terms possible and don't bother your head too much about those who undertake to raise the balance whether they have bonded it for much or little. I will tell you why. Under our law, except in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the amount of the bonded stock has nothing to-do with the fixing of the rates. If a case is brought before the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, the question to be decided there is what is the proper rate, and not what is the rate charged.
How would you ascertain a proper rate ?

Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Richardson) can answer, but it is one of the most difficult problems I know of. Some hon. gentlemen assume that the government or a railway commission can in some way decide off-hand, but these gentlemen have not studied the question or they would think differently. How are you going to say what is a fair rate ? I tell you that you will have to get an education that no man in this House has to-day before you can decide that.
I can tell you.

I have paid some attention to the question ; I have consulted men who have devoted their lives to it and I have read books upon it, and all agree that it is a most difficult problem, although I will agree with these lion, gentlemen that you have to watch the railways. But look at the condition of things in Canada. The fact is that the farmer in the most remote part of Ontario can land his produce in Liverpool cheaper than the farmer in Wales can send it to London. What do these gentleman say to that ? The truth is that the people of Canada wanted railways and were not afraid to assume responsibilities to get railways, and were willing to give men a fair margin of profit who took the risk of raising the necessary money to build these railways. There is not a country of the same population under heaven that has a better water or rail transportation system than has Canada. I just wish to say that, 271
in order to relieve myself of the depression which I might experience by listening to the pessimistic views of some gentlemen in this House. I made up my mind to say something upon the other side of the question. Let me say one word about the Canadian Pacific Railway and about this 10 per cent. Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Richardson, Lisgar) remember the difficulty there was in getting anybody to undertake the Canadian Pacific Railway ? Does he remember how earnestly and honestly the two political parties in the early days of that tremendous undertaking were concerned about that work; and does he remember that its initiation and successful carrying into effect would have paralyzed any small nation except Canada ? The hon. gentleman (Mr. Richardson) talked to-day about the lands in the North-west and he counts up their value by the millions. But how much were those lands worth before the Canadian Pacific Railway was constructed ? Why, we have under our control the alternate sections which, even if we gave for nothing to settlers who would go in there and develop them, are still a most valuable asset. I believe, Sir, that we made a good bargain with the Canadian Pacific Railway. What if we did give the Canadian Pacific Railway several millions, have we not a return for it ? I tell you that the enhanced credit of Canada at home and abroad by the successful carrying out of the Canadian Pacific Railway, is worth twice the number of millions we invested in it.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tisdale), stated that our North-west lands were worth nothing before the Canadian Pacific Railway was constructed. Does he not think that if the government built that road themselves with the money they gave the Canadian Pacific Railway that those lands would be just as valuable today ?

Certainly, but if the hon. gentleman had a political part to take in this House in those early days as he has to-day, would he have dared to say that Canada should have assumed that burden ? He dare not. The best men of both political parties, men who knew as much in those days as the best of us know to-day, agreed that things should have been done as they were done and the people of the country were satisfied. Had Canada not made that bargain her credit would not have been such in the interim as to enable her to carry out the other immense public works of the country. By giving the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway to men who could raise the money abroad, the Canadian Pacific Railway was constructed and the chances are that it might not have been constructed otherwise. You have to draw a distinction between things as they existed then and things as they exist at the present time. I will not

be any meaner as a public man than I am as a private citizen, and I say that even if we had made, which I deny, a bad bargain with tlie Canadian Pacific Railway, yet it was made in broad day light by the representatives of the people of Canada, and the bargain should be maintained to the letter. If we act in good faith we will maintain our self-respect and have a higher standing as a nation than if we act in bad faith, even though we made money by doing so. Whether it was a wise bargain' or not we should stick to it, and although we did cancel part of the contract, yet I believe that the Canadian Pacific Railway agreed to it at the time. I am no defender of the Canadian Pacific Railway people, and I have no reason to be particularly friendly with them. My interest has been in the railways in my own province, and if I have been more friendly to one railway than the other it has been to the old Grand Trunk which was the pioneer road in the older provinces, and which enabled us to build these local roads and to turn them over to a company that could handle them as we could not. It is to the credit of the Canadian Pacific Railway that they have gone outside of the mere operating of their main line, because had they done nothing more they would never have paid a cent on the money invested. But they have their telegraph lines, and their sleeping-cars, and their steamship lines, all auxiliaries to the main line and the earnings of which go into the same treasury and enable them to pay dividends. If there was nothing but the bare Canadian Pacific Railway, then notwithstanding all the money we gave them, I doubt if they would today be able to pay 2 per cent on the actual money they raised. Well, Sir, there are men who fought me in 3871 on the political question as to whether it was a wise thing to make the contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and have the road built, and I am glad I have lived to see them recant the views they then held. The prime minister of the province of Ontario ; one of the brightest men in that province-and I say it though he is politically opposed to me-he has acknowledged the mistake he made in opposing the Canadian Pacific Railway in the early days. I am not afraid to stand up here and bear testimony to a great corporation that has carried ou an immense work under the greatest difficulties, and has made a brillant record for this country. Let me tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Richardson) that in my opinion this railway commission might not be the unmixed blessing he thinks. We have evidences on every side that there is going to be discussion on this railway commission question in this parliament.
I have lately consulted a report of the commission that was appointed some years ago to consider this question. That commission was composed of able men, with Sir Alexander Galt as chairman. They took Mr. TISDALE.
the best expert evidence they could obtain as to the most efficient tribunal that would be available to control rates, railway disputes and similar matters; and they recommended the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. I think that body has administered its duties fairly well. I supported it when the Conservative party were in power, and I have supported it just as strongly since hon. gentlemen who are opposed to me politically have had charge of it. Why did the commission prefer that tribunal ? It would have several good features. It would be sure to be composed of able men, from whichever party they came ; and not only able men, but men responsible directly to the people for their places and for the way they administered their trust. They were given plenary powers. They had the absolute power to enforce their decisions, and even if necessary to order out a force for that purpose. It is impossible to have any other tribunal equal to it in these respects. You could not vest such powers in a railway commission, because it would be a reversal of our constitution to do so. Therefore, I sympathize with the members of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council in wishing to compel them to retain their present powers. I am quite sure they would be willing to resign the duties imposed upon them, and to place them upon other shoulders, but I do not think those duties would be as promptly or satisfactorily attended to. Further, there would be great difficulty in getting three men qualified to act on a railway commission. In the United States they have sometimes had these railway commissions, they have sometimes abolished them, and they have sometimes brought them back. So far as I am concerned, I am quite content with a Railway Committee of the Privy Council, composed of my political opponents, rather than relegate to a railway commission such as we could choose such powers as we could confer upon it.
The hon. gentleman did not understand me to give an unqualified endorsement to the appointment of a railway commission ?

I give an unqualified fealty to the present tribunal in preference to a commission. Having thus expressed myself, I do not wish hon. gentlemen to suppose that I do not think it wise to have this discussion. I do not want them to suppose that while I disagree with them, I am finding fault with them in any way. I am glad to see them bring up these questions for discussion, because that is the way to get light. But I prefer to go slow, and to hold by what we have found to be good rather than to take the chances of an untried experiment.

Mr. Speaker, this very important subject has been pretty thoroughly threshed out in

this House, not only this afternoon, but in previous sessions, and I had no idea that there was any possibility of a difference of opinion upon it anywhere in the Dominion of Canada. I had not thought that there was any person who would get up and earnestly combat the advisability of appointing some additional body, different from anything we have in the country at the present time, to regulate the operations of the railways. But the sentiments which have been expressed by the bon. gentleman who has just sat down (Hon. Mr. Tisdale), indicate that there is an opposition in the country and in this House to the idea of the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis). I notice that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) applied the term pessimist to the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson.)
I did not apply to any individual, nor to this proposition. The hon. gentleman misunderstood me.

I understood the hon. gentleman to apply the term to those who hold the ideas expressed in this resolution. I am one of those myself. I think the hon. gentleman himself is a worse pessimist than we are, because we express the view that certain conditions may be improved. I do not understand that the hon. gentleman disputed the facts set out by the hon. member for Saskatchewan and the hon. member for Lisgar ; but he has no idea that any improvement in existing conditions is possible. Therefore, I think he is the worse pessimist. One opinion the hon. gentleman expressed was that if was impossible under our constitution for such a body as that suggested to be created and to perform any valuable service. To meet that point, I think it is only necessary to refer to one of the facts stated by the hon. member for Saskatchewan-the fact that in the mother country, the land from which we get our constitution, some such body as that suggested was created, and existed for a number of years, and is still in operation. If it is not impossible in England, it cannot be impossible in Canada, for our constitution is very similar to that of Great Britain. Another point which the hon. gentleman raised was the difficulty in the way of reducing freight rates, owing to the very low interest which stockholders in railway companies have been able to reap since railways have been operated in this country. That is perfectly true, I believe, even of some of the lines of railway in the North-west Territories which have been referred to this afternoon by the hon. member for Saskatchewan and the hon. member for Lisgar. Take, for instance, the Calgary and Edmonton road. I believe the stockholders in that road, at least the present managers, are having great difficulty in earning sufficient from the operation of the road to pay the interest on
the existing bonds. It is perfectly true that these stockholders are in this difficulty, that they cannot get a fair rate of interest on their investment. But what is the reason ? It is to be found in the insane method by which the roads were built and the corporations created. If the stockholders have difficulties to meet, certainly there were some promoters who had no difficulty at all in making a very good rate of interest on their investment, because, as has been stated, the Calgary and Edmonton road was constructed in such a manner that its promoters did not put a single cent into it, and were able besides to put into their pockets an amount almost equal to that which the road cost. The country kindly gave the promoters, not only the amount which the road cost, but a duplicate amount to put into their pockets.
This is not a new question, but one which lias been pretty thoroughly and widely discussed. The conditions existing with respect to excessive and discriminating freight rates are pretty generally admitted. Even the hon. gentleman who last spoke did not dispute any of the statements made by the two hon. gentlemen who preceded him ; and admitting the facts, it is evident that the government will have to take the matter up and try and devise a remedy. This subject has been already discussed this session.
I am bound to admit that I am inclined to a certain extent, to favour some of the views expressed here since this session opened, by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), who is not here this afternoon, and quite ready to admit that I am in favour of the principle of government ownership and operation of railways in Canada. But I must also confess that I lack some of the faith with which my hon. friend from East York is blessed. I lack faith in the idea that $2 taken out of the treasury of Canada would be sufficient to secure government control of all the railways in Canada, and I possibly lack a little of the faith of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson), who has spoken this afternoon. I have very grave doubts as to whether government ownership is a practical immediate remedy. While the people in the Territories are suffering from excessive railway rates, they are also suffering from lack of railroads. While one of the needs of the North-west Territories is lower freight rates, another is a greater mileage of railways. We have settlements in that country, which have been waiting seventeen or eighteen years for railway communication, and which to-day are still distant sixty or seventy miles from any railway. Unless this parliament is willing this year or next year to accept the principle of government ownership and operation of railways and apply that principle immediately, I would not confine myself to advocating that remedy alone. I hope and trust that, with the assistance of the Minister of

Railways, some of tliose people who have been waiting for railway communication during so many years, and who settled under the definite promise, given by those in authority at that time, that railway communication would be furnished them at an early day, will find their expectations realized very shortly.
The hon. gentleman who spoke last (Mr. Tisdale) did not dispute any of the facts presented by the two hon. gentlemen who preceded him. It is entirely unnecessary for me to take up the time of the House by supplementing these facts. I will confine myself to relating one instance which came under my own notice. Some months ago a firm in Vancouver ordered a piece of machinery from Glasgow, Scotland, and about the same time a firm in Regina ordered an identical piece of machinery from the same people manufactured in the very same place. Would you believe it, Sir, when I tell you that the piece of machinery laid down in Regina cost in freight within a few cents of $100 more than the piece of machinery laid down in Vancouver, 1,500 miles farther away. That is an instance of what the people in the North-west Territories have to complain of.
One of the points raised by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson), which would tend to lessen our faith in the proposition submitted by the non. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), namely, the establishment of a railway commission, is the existence of what is known as the 10 per cent clause in the agreement between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the government. That is something which must remain there until eliminated by purchase or some other means, and which would limit the power that a railway commission would have over the railway company. But even taking that objection into account, there is in Manitoba and the North-west a considerable mileage of railways not covered by that contract and to which, consequently, that 10 per cent clause does not apply. 'l do not think I am very wide of the mark when 1 say that there are probably a thousand miles of railway west of Lake Superior, between Lake Superior and the Rocky Mountains, to which that clause does not apply.
If the statements made by the hon. member for Saskatchewan respecting rates on the branch line from Regina to Prince Albert are true, then there is good reason, even though the commission could not touch the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, to consider whether a commission should not be appointed to control rates on the thousand miles of road not under the ten pel cent clause. However. I was somewhat surprised to hear the objection raised by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson), because I recollect that last year or the year before, when some other railway contract was up in this House for discussion, he suggested inserting in the contract a provision

embodying exactly the principle embodied in this ten per cent clause. He went over the ground this afternoon establishing the fact that my recollection was accurate and that he had moved for the insertion of this provision limiting the returns to six per cent- the difference between six per cent and ten per cent being not one of principle, but of detail. I do not intend to take up the time of the House at greater length. But if this House and the government admit the facts presented, they must, in all reason, apply their minds to find a remedy. If this House and the government state that government ownership does not afford an immediate, a practicable remedy, then let us be told what is such a remedy. If the government and the House hold that such a commission as is now suggested will not constitute a practicable and effective remedy, then let us be told in what way an adequate remedy may be found. Surely if we admit the conditions, if we admit the fact of these discriminations imposed upon the people of the west-and if what the newspapers state be true, the evil does not exist exclusively in the west, but the people of the eastern provinces have reason also to complain- it is the duty of this government and the duty of this parliament to find a remedy and apply it as speedily as possible.

It is not necessary to add anything to what has been said in proof of the necessity of a railway commission whose duty it would be to adjust fairly the rates as between shippers and as between different localities. All I wish to say is, that while a railway commission is necessary, in my humble opinion, towards remedying the present conditions, it does not and cannot, in the nature of things, provide a complete remedy for those conditions. Some of those conditions, I am afraid, have gone beyond remedy. But the fact that there are or may be such conditions as cannot be remedied makes it all the more necessary that we should provide against the recurrence of like conditions in all eases in the future over which we have control, and with the responsibility for which we are charged. The point has probably been alluded to by other speakers, but I wish to emphasize it, that the great difficulty we have, or shall have, in dealing with the question of rates on our railroad system is the fact that the railroads of the country have been permitted to be overloaded with indebtedness. In view of that circumstance, and in view of the facts laid before the House, I desire to place before hon. members the great and urgent necessity of providing against over-capitalization of all railroads chartered by this House in future. I hold that if this House allows railroads to be bonded on the basis of their possible earning power, instead of requiring that they should be bonded only on the basis of their cost, this House cannot

afterwards come in and regulate the rates below the point that will permit those roads to earn a fair interest on the amount of indebtedness which has been incurred with the consent of this House. We should provide in all railroad charters hereafter granted that indebtedness should not be allowed beyond the cost of the road. Then, we pay for what we get and we get what we pay for. We know that we cannot have railroads without money. Our complaint against present conditions is not that we are required to pay interest on the cost of the roads, but it is that we are required to pay interest on double and treble the cost of the roads ; and we ask that for the future we shall be ensured that, whatever the railroad may cost, it is only on that cost that we shall be required to pay interest in the way of railway rates.
Now, as there have been instances given of peculiar rates, I wish to draw attention to an instance also, the more particularly because this is in connection with the rates over the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, a railway the rates on which, we were given to understand, the government absolutely controlled. I have a memorandum placed in my hands which purports to give the local rates charged over that road, between certain points previous to May, 1900, and since May, 1900. I find that, from Lethbridge to Cranbrook, previous to May, 1900, the first-class rate was 99 cents per hundred pounds; second class, 82 cents ; third class, 65 cents : fourth class, 49 cents ; fifth class, 44 cents ; and tenth class, 22 cents. I find that since May 14, 1900, the rates have been : first class, $1.27 per hundred pounds ; second class, $1.06 ; third class, 85 cents ; fourth class, 64 cents; fifth class, 58 cents ; and tenth class, 29 cents. The people who live along that line of road very naturally asked the question, and I may tell the House and the minister that they asked it very pertinently during the election, how, if this government had control of the rates over that road, they permitted that increase to be made. I was not able to answer them, and I ask the Minister of Railways now : Has the government, as a matter of fact, control over those rates, and if it has, what were the reasons which led them to permit this increase of rates to take place 7 I think anybody will agree, upon comparing the rates previous to May, 1900, over the Crow's Nest line, with similar rates in other parts of the country, that those rates were certainly high enough. But they were increased very materially after May 14, and the people along that line, and I, as their representative in this House, want to know whether that increase was made in defiance of the government or with the consent of the government.

Before the question is put, I would like to make a few remarks on this subject. I
think that the public at any rate look for some measure of government control, or at least for a commission that should to a certain extent control the rates. Personally, I am not acquainted with the grievances that are claimed to exist in regard to inequalities in freight rates, but I have seen a good deal of discussion about them in the public press. Those of us who have paid any attention to this question will have noticed in the press lately a number of articles concerning the practice of discrimination in freight rates on the part of railway companies. It occurs to me that the forms of discrimination, if they do exist, have more bearing upon the interests of the North-west and Manitoba than upon those of the province of Ontario.
In this connection we are reminded of the discussions that took place when the original contract was made with the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Liberal party at that time contended that under the proposed contract certain evils would arise in the future that would cause a great deal of difficulty and a great deal of trouble; and people are apparently realizing now that these evils prophesied by the Liberal party are actually upon them. But, there is no doubt that the people look for some measure of redress; and I am sometimes of the opinion, whether wrongly or rightly, that the people of the North-west, judging by the arguments that are advanced, look for the same consideration and the same rates as the people of the older settled provinces. It strikes me that many of the arguments advanced by the people of the North-west tend to put the matter upon the same footing as in the older settled portions of the country, and they are asking for the same consideration. Now, I am not saying that the Canadian Pacific Railway discriminates, but all their arguments seem to be directed against the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway may deserve the criticisms levelled against it or it may not; all I can say is that the undertaking of constructing that railway was one of enormous magnitude. But people seem to be looking for some form of redress whereby the grievances that they claim to suffer may be removed. I understand that a system has been in vogue in the old country for a number of years, introduced away back in the early fifties, which might be some guide to us. A commission was appointed for a period of five years, and proved so successful that it has been repeatedly reappointed and exists, I understand, at the present time. In the neighbouring republic we find railway commissions existing that are endowed with certain powers to adjust grievances between the people and the railway companies, and to supervise rates and deal with attempted discriminations. Apparently these commissions have proved successful there, and it is possible a similar commission might prove successful in this country.

The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) made a remark that the public expected the Dominion government to deal with questions of this kind, and if the government do not deal with them the public will deal with the government. There is a certain amount of force in that. I am not prepared to go quite as far as the hon. gentleman does along that line, but the public no doubt look to the Dominion government to take some steps, or to enact some legislation, to bring about a better state of affairs than exists at the present time. I am not a very extensive shipper, so personally, I have no grievance to complain of; but parties who are large shippers have complained to me at different times that unfair discrimination is made by the roads, discrimination which they cannot overcome. They have no court of appeal, and they have no way of redressing their grievance, and consequently have had to submit to them so far. It seems to me that some measure of this kind might well be introduced into this country. So far as my opinion goes it leans toward a government commission.
I do not propose to go into the side issues, so to speak, bearing upon this question further than to make a passing remark in reference to government ownership of railways. I am not yet sufficiently advanced to give my consent to government ownership of railways. I think, however, I can foresee a good many difficulties in connection with the successful management of railways by the government. I have noticed that the arguments advanced by members on the other side of the House, with the exception of the hon. member for Lisgar, with respect to government ownership of railways, have come largely from men who were instrumental in fastening upon the North-west, the very railway that they are trying to get control of now, men who, in their papers or in their arguments on the floor of the House, were instrumental in fastening upon the North-west the very objectionable system that they are to-day asking this government to assume control of, and to use for the benefit of the people. I do not believe that the principle of government ownership of railways is theoretically correct; it seems to me there are a great many grave dangers in connection with it. I am satisfied that the people in the western part of Ontario, as well as in other portions of the province, are by no means united in favour of the principle of government ownership of railways. It seems to me that the easier solution of the difficulty might be in some form of legislation like the appointment of a railway commission or tribunal of some sort that can deal with matters of this kind.

I rise to say very briefly that I am in favour of a commission, as moved for by the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis). I Mr. HOLMES.
believe that the time has arrived when, if the government cannot see its way clear to purchase and manage the railways of this country, they certainly ought to appoint a commission of able men to manage the railways irrespective of party politics. The farmers' gatherings all through the country, In Ontario, at least, have expressed themselves strongly upon this matter, and they are all desirous of a commission being appointed for the purpose of settling differences between the people and the railways, and preventing discrimination in favour of exporters or importers and against the farmers. We have heard four hon. gentlemen from the North-west Territories and Manitoba speak this afternoon in favour of the appointment: of a commission. They are all suffering from the effects of the overcharges of the railways. I am satisfied that Ontario lias a grievance, especially when the railway companies will carry freight to the seaboard at a cheaper rate than from a point in Ontario. The Grand Trunk Railway will carry freight as cheaply from Chicago to the seaboard as from Listowei. There must be something wrong when railway companies are allowed to discriminate against the farmers of Ontario in favour of the farmers of the North-west Territories and the farmers of tlie United States. I think something should be done, and done quickly. The country is expecting this government to do something. I believe it has been promised. I believe the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) has stated that something of this kind will be done, and the people are looking for it. I have nothing more to say except that I fully endorse the motion that has been made by the hou. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) and supported by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) and others.

Mr. Speaker,
I was going to suggest that there are a couple of hon. gentlemen who would like very much to say something upon this motion, but who are not in the Chamber at this moment, and perhaps it may be agreeable to the House to call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the House took recess. After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speakeroldname: Mr. WILLIAM A. GALLIHER (Yale and Cariboo).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reference to the motion before the House, I would like to add a few words to those which have already been said by hon. members before me. I live in the western part of the country myself and represent a western constituency.
I have personally experienced the hardships that have been complained of so much in regard to excessive rates, and have done so for the past twenty years. I do not propose, for my part, to abuse the Canadian

Pacific Railway here to-night, or any other railway company. We are all more or less proud of that great transcontinental line known as the Canadian Pacific Railway, hut, at the same time, it behooves us to watch carefully and see that the road is giving us justice and giving us justice in every respect. Although this question has been threshed thread bare in this House, and we can hardly expect to have any fresh light on the matter until some practical plan is submitted to the House, yet I wish to express my opinion very briefly upon it. My predecessor in the representation of Winnipeg, the late Mr. Jameson, introduced a motion similar to this one in 1898. He referred to the fact that the government had promised to bring down some kind of measure providing for a railway commission, and he excused himself in speaking to the motion on the ground that his remarks might probably prepare the minds of hon. gentlemen for the expected measure. Now, it seems to me that the railway question in the country has made a great deal more progress than the questions of a railway commission in this House. There is need for some stronger control over our railways than we have now ; some government supervision, some-

thing that will bring the railways nearer together in the matter of rates and abolish that discrimination which is so rampant all over the country. Cases of discrimination have been presented to this House so many times that there is hardly need to refer to them, but one very flagrant case in connection with the furniture trade has come to my notice. On a car-load of chairs from Ontario to Vancouver, the rate is $1.17 ; on a car-load of bedroom suites the rate is $1.38 ; on a car-load of mixed furniture the rate is $1.68 ; and if there be included in it any upholstered goods the rate is $2.08. It is plain that this discriminates against the small dealers and in favour of the big dealer, who can order a car-load of each kind of article.
