The effect of this discrimination is to absolutely prohibit that small dealer from buying Canadian goods and rather than pay the high freight rates, it is cheaper for him to buy in the western states and pay freight and duty on the goods that he sells to Canadian citizens on the Pacific coast. In spite of all the difficulties that have to be overcome, I have hope that a railway commission can accomplish some good, because in ten or a dozen states of the union where railway commissions have been operating from ten to twenty years, satisfactory results have accrued to the farming and business communities. At the same time, I must say that I do not believe that the appointment of a railway commission will ever prove a proper solution of the transportation problem in Canada. That, in my opinion, can only be attained by government ownership of the roads. At the present lime the people of the country have to bear all the burdens of the construction and of the operation of these railways, and, sometimes they have to bear the cost of maladministration, and yet we practically have no say at all in their management, and no control over their rates. If I believed that the appointment of a railway commission would in any way militate against progress in the line of government ownership, I would not be in favour of it, because I do not believe that a railway commission will be a final solution of the difficulties that have to be overcome in this transportation question. The very extent of our country demands that we should look to finality in this matter, and the only way we can govern the roads effectively is by government ownership, operation, and control.

Many years ago, when this question was first introduced to the notice of the Canadian parliament by Mr. Dalton McCarthy, then member for Simeoe, I supported it. There was a growing feeling in the country that some competent power should control the railways and adjust disputes between the railway companies and the shippers throughout Canada. The agitation grew stronger from Mr. PUTTEE.
year to year, both in this House and in the country, until the government were obliged to ignore it no longer. Then a commission was appointed to inquire into these troubles and to ascertain what would be the best remedy. As a result of the report of that commission, the Railway Committee of the Privy Council was established. I held then, as I have ever believed since, that that was only a makeshift with a view of causing the agitation to subside, and to leave the railways still under the control of parliament. It seemed to me that the railway companies had some kind of cinch upon the parliament of the day, so that they felt safer in the hands of parliament, than under the control of an independent commission, and from that time onwards such cases as have been brought to the notice of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council have been adjusted by that body. As to the workableness of that body, and as to whether it has fulfilled the expectations of the people, it is unnecessary for me to say much at the present time, because the country knows as well as I do that the Railway Committee of the Privy Council has failed to meet the expectations or desires of the people, or to give the people confidence in the tribunal.
The hon. member for South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) expressed the opinion very strongly that a railway commission would be an unworkable body in this country, and referred to the fact that railway commissions in the United States had not done all that was expected of them. But when speaking of that subject, I thought he did not display a very intimate knowledge of what had been accomplished in the United States through railway commissions. If he had been as familiar with the workings of those commissions as some United States writers, he would have, at least, conceded a great deal of good had been accomplished by them -that while they failed to do all that was expected of them, it could not be successfully established that they were a failure. Where they were a partial failure, it is for us to inquire what were the causes of failure, and whether those causes would apply with equal force in Canada. In my judgment they would not. The principal cause of their failure in the United States was the fact that different states were governed by state laws, so that when a railway passed beyond the boundary of one state, it came under a different law. But that is no reason why the same difficulty would be met with here. We have no provincial laws that would interfere with the working of a commission, because all our railways are largely under the control of the Dominion ; and a railway commission which had its authority from this parliament would be able to exercise a very effectual control over them in every part of the country. But the history of railway commissions in the United States-and I

have taken some trouble to look into it-is that they have been of very great benefit to the people, remedying many grievances, and readjusting many difficulties between railway companies and the people, in many cases to the satisfaction of both.
The hon. member for South Norfolk rather read to the House a lecture on the subject of interference with railway companies. The hon. gentleman said that we hear the pessimistic utterances of men against railway companies-companies who bond railways for very large amounts of money and then complain when we endeavour to readjust the tariff of rates on these railways, and point out that they are not earning a fair rate of interest on ithe money invested in them. Lest I should do the hon. gentleman injustice, 1 will quote his own words as I took them down : ' We are talking about conditions and difficulties of railway problems of which we know little,' and he went on to give us a history of the difficulties encountered in promoting railway construction twenty-five or thirty years ago.
I remember when the hon. gentleman was one of the most active railway promoters in western Canada, and I know that he had many difficulties to contend with at that time. But the hon. member should not forget that we are a progressive people, and are advancing all the time. It was much more difficult to get capital to invest in railway construction then than it is to-day. The difficulty that existed then does not exist now. While to-day capital is plentiful, and a great deal of money is going into, railway construction, it is, to my mind, a matter of great importance to control the bonding power of these railways because the railway companies always put up the plea, when an agitation is started for a reduction of freight rates, that they are not earning a reasonable interest on the money invested. When such a plea is set up, it seems to me that it is the absolute duty of parliament to see that these railway companies are not loaded down with bonds and watered stock to a much greater amount than actually went into the construction of the roads. What we want to know about a particular road is, what amount of money actually went into its construction. The capitalist who put his money in is entitled to a fair interest upon it; but it cannot be successfully established that we are in duty bound to protect capitalists who have watered the stock, and who desire to get out of a road what they never put into it.
We cannot shut our eyes to the agitation which exists in the country to-day, which is becoming more strong and widespread, which is growing with such rapidity as will soon compel parliament to take note of it and deal with this vexed problem. It must be dealt with in the near future, and the government which is not capable of dealing with it will be obliged to give place to one
that will deal with it, and deal with it successfully.
The hon. gentleman gave us an illustration of what he regarded as unfair freight rates compared with what the farmer is getting to-day. He says the farmer in the most westerly portion of Canada pays less on his produce shipped to Liverpool than the farmer around Liverpool gets his goods taken to London. Whose grievance is that ? It is the grievance of the farmer around Liverpool, and let him fight his own batles. That has nothing to do with our grievances in this country. The hon. member for Western Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) made the statement, which, I presume, is capable of proof, that on a piece of machinery brought from Glasgow and laid down at Regina there was over $100 more paid for freight than is charged on a like article carried several hundred miles further and landed in British Columbia. Why should that be the case V
Because there is competition.

I hope that when the parliament of Canada puts money into railway enterprises, it is acting for the whole people of Canada, and the people have a right to expect that they will get fair-play in proportion to the distance of the haul. I am told that the railway problem is a complex one, requiring years of experience to understand, and that if a railway did not often haul goods long distances below actual cost, it would not get the business at all. Far better not get the business than do it under cost. When the western farmer had the privilege of carrying a barrel of flour from Minneapolis to Montreal at 25 cents a barrel, while the farmer of western Ontario had to give a share of hi? hard earnings to build a railway, and in addition was compelled to pay 35 cents for the hauling of a barrel of flour to Montreal, I say that Canada is paying its money for the benefit of the western farmer near St. Paul, rather than for the benefit of the farmer of western Ontario. Then, I am told in the same breath that it did not pay the actual cost of transportation. If it did not, why should we pay a part of that cost ? Is it to help to bring the western farmers around Minneapolis and St. Paul 500 miles, nearly 1.000 miles, nearer the market in which they sell their produce than we do the Canadian farmers here ?
This question must be dealt with in the near future. The sentiment in favour of settling it is growing so strong that the government cannot ignore it much longer.
The hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) said that the establishment of a railway commission would be an interference with the constitution. How would it interfere with the constitution ? There can be no interference with our constitutional rights in the appointment of a railway commission. 'No parliamentarian or

statesman will deny that we have the power and the right to establish such a commission without thereby violating in any degree the spirit of the constitution. It is just as much within our rights to do this as to make any other law for the purpose of controlling the railway companies.
I was rather amused at the illustration given us by the hon. member for Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher), of the discrimination in rates on the Crow's Nest Pass Railway. That brought to my mind the strong plea of the hon. the Minister of Railways in favour of giving that road a subsidy of $11,000 per mile, namely, that it would provide the farmer with reduced freight rates, and that the control of the freight rates would be in the hands of the government, and there would be no danger of discrimination. That was the plea he gave to justify the large subsidy of $11,000 per mile, and the illustration given by the hon. member for Yale and Cariboo now shows how little credence that plea was entitled to. The hon. member, by his argument, justified the contention on this side of the House that there was not sufficient provision made for the control of the freight rates by the government, and not sufficient justification for the large subsidy given that company.
The hon. member for South Norfolk said that we had no reason to bother ourselves at all about the bonding of the roads so long as the railways were built. That seems a very short-sighted policy for an hon. gentleman of Ills experience to advocate. It seems to be that we are bound to take, cognizance of the bonding of these roads, and keep it within reasonable bounds. Otherwise should we ever take the power to in any way control these railway corporations, we will find ourselves confronted with the same dilemma in which we are with the Canadian Pacific Railway to-day, and will be told that we must not do anything which would prevent any company paying the interest on its bonds, and on its watered stock, as well as on the money that actually went into the construction of the road. Are there any members here who know anything about the Great North-west Central Railway Company, which has a Bill before the House to-day ? If there are, they will remember that in the course of twenty years we were obliged, on two or three occasions, to provide, when amending the charter of that railway, that the company which took it up would furnish the money to pay its debts. There were thousands of dollars piled up against that road before a mile of it was in operation or even built. Another example is the Baie des Chaleurs Railway. Where did the money go which was voted for that railway by the Dominion government and the government of the province of Quebec V Should we ask that company to lower its freight rates, they would claim that they must be allowed to charge sufficiently high Mr. SPROULE.
rates to pay the interest on this money, or otherwise we would be doing an injustice to its creditors. Had we exercised the proper control over the expenditure of capital by these companies, and not have allowed them to squander it as they did, we would not be confronted with the dilemma in which we are to-day. Then there is the Atlantic and Lake Superior Company which has been before the country for many years. I give these examples to show the unwisdom of allowing railway companies to borrow money on bonds, and distribute it among railway promoters and charter brokers and others, and then have it charged up against the road as a debt, to meet the interest on which it is entitled to charge heavier freight rates than otherwise would be required. I give this as an answer to the hon. member for South Norfolk, that we should not concern ourselves at all about what the companies bond their road for, or how they water their stock or pile up debt.
We are rapidly reaching a day when one of two things must be accomplished. Either the government must control the railway companies, or the railway companies will emphatically and entirely control the government. Some people think they are doing that to-day. I am glad to see that occasionally our Minister of Railways puts up apparently a pretty good fight against them, but whether they are too strong or he fails to keep up the persistence absolutley necessary to success, the result seems to fall far short of his expectations. He, however, has my encouragement to any extent he can be induced to go in opposing the pretensions of these corporations.
I am not one of those who believe that a railway commission would remedy all the evils from which we are suffering. There are many reasons why it would not, but if it remedies only a tenth of the evils complained of, that would amply justify its creation. If the commission does not come up to what we expect, it will be easy to amend it. We know that the railway commissions in the United States have been beneficial in many respects, and we have more reason to expect success in this country because our railways are nearly all Dominion roads, and we are not hampered by any state laws as these commissions are in the United States. It is said that as our railways extend in the United States and draw considerable traffic from there, a railway commission would not be effective. But that argument would apply with tenfold greater force to railway commissions in the United States, where each state has its own railway legislation.
I think it would be workable to a greater extent than many people suppose. While I do not believe it would entirely cure the evil we have to contend with, I think it would be a step in the right direction. But there

is one thing sure, and that is that in the near future something must he done. Some tell us that the remedy should be the purchase and ownership of the railways by the state. That seems a gigantic undertaking, and one for which we are hardly prepared.
1 have sometimes thought that we should bring our efforts to bear in a way of increasing our own railway by extending the government railway to the lakes, and ultimately it might reach the Pacific coast. This would give us the through railway that would offer a salutary check upon the two great corporations that seem likely, in the near future, to control all the railways of the country. Such a project involves a much smaller financial undertaking than the buying out of all the railways, and I would rather favour that. But I must say that there is a growing feeling that the day will come when the state will be obliged, in some way, to take charge of the railways, or to have control of them by purchase or otherwise. But, for the present, let us make a step in advance of what we have done in the past. It seems to me the only reasonable thing would be the establishment of a proper railway commission to do the work very largely on the same lines as those followed by a similar tribunal in the United States.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to have spoken on this question to-night, as I had no notice until this afternoon that the subject was coming up. This is a question the history of which is practically the history of Manitoba and the North-west Territories for the last twenty years ; it is a question calling for thought and preparation on the part of one who is to speak upon it. I will not weary the House with details of cases of discrimination in freight or passenger rates or excessive rates charged by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, for I believe these matters have been thoroughly dealt with by previous speakers. But I would refer to one or two phases of the question that, it seems to me, have not been sufficiently dealt with. Several speakers who preceded me have told you that grants have been given to the Canadian Pacific both in cash and in public lands. They forgot, however, to mention that these lands have been free from taxes ever since they were given to the Canadian Pacific Company, which, if translated into terms of money, would represent a very large sum. These hon. gentlemen forgot to tell you that these lands have been increased in value, not, as one hon. gentleman said this afternoon, by the fact of the line being built, but by immigrants coming in and settling on the homestead lands alongside, improving them, and building roads, bridges, schools, and so on.
As I have said, the history of the Canadian Pacific Railway is almost contemporaneous with that of Manitoba for the last
twenty years, and it would be well to refer back to 1881 and to speeches made by members of this House at that time, some of whom are still here. I regret that time has not permitted me to refer to the debates on that occasion. Asj a resident of Winnipeg, however, I can remember looking over the newspapers at the time, and scanning the reports of speeches of the leaders on either side. I can remember that the leaders of the opposition of that day made most strenuous efforts to have certain clauses inserted in the contract which were not accepted by parliament. And it is for that reason that we suffer some of the grievances we are labouring under to-day. I can recollect certain prophecies made by Sir Charles Tupper -I was going to say 'promises,' but I remember that Sir Charles Tupper denied that lie had made promises and said that they were prophecies. He prophesied in 1881 that, in ten years from the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, there .would be two million people in that country, and we would export, if I remember the figures well, 60,000,000 bushels of wheat per year. No part of that prophecy has ever been fulfilled. I regret to say that the census of 1891 showed very small advance over the natural increase of the population for the ten years between 1881 and 1891. When Sir Charles Tupper made that prophecy in this House, I feel assured, he honestly stated what he believed. I believe that that hon. gentleman was, in most of his acts, a friend of the west. I believe that when he was a member of this House, and also when he was High Commissioner in England, his intentions were honestly friendly to the western country. But I believe that, unknowingly, he placed in the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway a weapon by which his prophecies were defeated. The first difficulty arose when the Canadian Pacific Railway Company gave the construction of the road to a company composed of their own managers. The first steal, if we may use the term, was made when this construction company made millions of dollars out of the building of the road, which stands charged to the people of Manitoba to-day. The next difficulty arose in 1884-I believe, when, as you know, the farmers' union was formed in Manitoba-many farmers in Manitoba began to see that the road which was to have been of so much benefit to us was a monopoly that would take the profit of everything they raised. I remember attending a meeting of that union in the Opera House in Winnipeg. I saw men there take off their coats and make speeches of a most declamatory and inflammatory nature-almost to the extent of threatening war. I afterwards saw many of the men who attended that meeting, among them some of the most solid farmers of the province, go to Minnesota and Dakota to escape this octopus whose tentacles were closing around them-and many of them can be found in those states to-day. It went on

till 1886, If I recollect aright, when the merchants of Winnipeg and the farmers of the west saw that this Canadian Pacific Railway, unless there was some competition in rates, would take the profits of everything in the country-that everything would belong to that company. We clamoured for lines to be brought in from the south. The hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) said this afternoon that the Canadian Pacific charter had been altered in 1886 so as to allow other lines to come in. And how did that come about ? If you had been at a place called Fort White, near Winnipeg, at that time, Mr. Speaker, you would know why they had allowed other lines in. You would have seen citizens there, church members, peaceful men, standing at that crossing where the diamond was being put in at two o'clock in the morning, with something in their hip-pockets besides tooth-picks-and they meant business. When the box-car of the Canadian Pacific Railway with forty men aboard came up to that diamond, those men saw that the safest thing for them was to get out! of the car. Time has gone on, but Sir Charles Tupper's prophecies are far from being fulfilled. I claim that one of the greatest causes retarding immigration into the North-west has been this Canadian Pacific Company. I must do them the justice of saying that during the last three or four years they have made some concessions to passengers going into Manitoba and the North-west Territories from the south. They have also given a pretty low rate on freight that is settlers' effects-a $6 rate on car-load lots from the boundary line to Winnipeg. The Northern Pacific Company does the same. They have also given a low rate to Edmonton-about $42- on car-load lots, and also a low rate on passenger traffic. But when the immigrant wants to go back to see his friends, he has to pay four cents a mile, and an exorbitant freight rate on everything he wants to take out. You can easily imagine the effect that it will have ujton jteople coming from the United States, and from the old country as well. Some Russians, for instance, who have come in the last five or six years, after they have been accustomed to travel at the rate of one-third of a cent per mile at home, when they are told that they have got to pay four cents, they walk. That is the way they get over the difficulty. The same plan is followed by some merchants living down in the country not far from Winnipeg, in the town of Selkirk, twenty miles away. I have known them to employ teams of horses to draw their groceries, coal oil and so forth, instead of taking them by railway. They say they can make more money that way than by paying the Canadian Pacific Railway rates.
Now. I would like to discover the best means for relieving the province of Manitoba and the west generally of this condition of affairs. It is a matter that will Mr. McCreary.
require considerable thought. Government ownership is a very popular cry. It is a fad in the minds of some people. But the difficulty is that it has not yet been tried in Canada sufficiently to warrant any man of sound judgment in saying it is going to be an unqualified success. I have had a little experience in municipal matters, and for a number of years, in our city of Winnipeg, we worked for municipal ownership of public franchises, when I was a member of the city council in 1895, 1896 and 1897, we undertook to municipalize our waterworks. We raised three-quarters of a million dollars under a by-law, and went into that scheme. I am sorry to say, and my hon. friend across the floor, from Lisgar, will bear me out, that these waterworks have not been the success I should like to have seen them. I believe the principal is all right, but unfortunately one thing and another has happened so that the people are not altogether satisfied with the result. We must also say that the management of the Intercolonial Railway for the last twenty years, or for the last number of years, has not been so satisfactory to the people of Canada as it should have been. I very much fear that according to our present system of government it may be some time before we reach that millennial stage by which government ownership of railways will be in the best interest of the people. I very much fear that so long as party government prevails in its present hard and fast lines, no matter how religious and pious party politicians may be in power, they will be too much disposed to favour their own friends and make the railway management a political lever, for such management to be in the best interests of the public. All these matters have got to be taken into consideration before we should have government ownership. I observe with some pleasure that the Hon. Geo. W. Ross proposes or suggests to construct a line of railway to Temiscamingue. I would like to see this experiment tried in the province of Ontario, before it is attempted in the great Dominion.
I believe that a railway commission properly conducted will be the means of doing much good, but I think a great deal depends upon the powers of that commission.
I trust that the commission will not be empowered merely to settle questions of discriminations in rates, I trust that it will not be limited to settling time tables and matters of that sort; but that it will have such powers as will enable it to go back and examine this charter given to the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1881, and to consult the best attorneys, irrespective of any railway company that can be found, to see exactly what the meaning of that charter is. A charter has sometimes to be studied, to be read very closely, and several times before the full gist of it is comprehended, and I take it, that if solicitors of ability were to take up that charter and to look up that

clause which seems to trouble the hon. member for Lisgar so much, they might find means of getting over that ten per cent clause. I would not be surprised if solicitors could even find means of getting over that. I recollect very well we had a charter given to a street railway company in the city of Winnipeg, and some years ago the company refused to level their tracks with the street crossings. They refused to do several other things that the city engineer required of them. He gave them a notice as required by the charter and they refused to comply. Another solicitor was called in, and I pointed out to him clause two of the charter, and I said :	Doesn't that
clause mean that if they won't carry out this thing you can take away their charter? A bill in equity was filed within two or three weeks to take away their charter, and they came down off their perch immediately and did whatever the city of Winnipeg required of them. For years the city of Winnipeg had no idea they had such power.
There is no doubt that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, if properly brought to task, will do much better than they are doing to-day. This is borne out by a statement made the other day by Mr. Sliauglmessy, president of the road, when Mr. Roblin, now premier of Manitoba, brought in a Bill to purchase the Northern Pacific Railway, to guarantee its bonds and to make a certain bargain with the Canadian Northern road. Immediately we saw Mr. Sliauglmessy come to the legislature and say :	Don't do this for God's sake, I
will come down, I will give you a reduction of four cents within the short space of two years if you will not give this charter to that company. That shows what can be done if the people of Manitoba are in earnest. Now, Sir, I believe that this commission will not fulfil probably all that is expected of it, it will not carry out everything that we require. But, I believe it is a step in the right direction, and after we have had it two or three years, and find that it is not relieving the west of the disabilities under which they are labouring, then will be the time for the western politicians, irrespective of party, to .loin hands and hearts and come down to eastern Canada and to this parliament and demand that the government build such roads as will enable our new province and the western territories to achieve the destiny for which they were carved out.

If you will permit me, Mr. Speaker, I desire to add something that the hon. gentleman has omitted. He said that government ownership had not been tried sufficiently in this country to warrant any man of sense and judgment advocating it. It may be that what he says is correct. But government ownership has been tried successfully in Austria-Hungary, in Belgium, in Switzerland, in Germany and in the Australasian
colonies, and so far as figures go, has proved to be an absolute success.
i was speaking of Canada. The conditions may be so different in those European countries that they would not apply here at all.

I do not rise to take part In this discussion, but merely to put myself on record. I come from the eastern part of Canada, where we have the advantages or disadvantages of a state-owned railway, and for one I desire to say that I think the advantages entirely outweigh the disadvantages. A great many of our people are in sympathy with the desire of the west for state-owned roads. Now it has been made apparent here that the people are suffering from undue exactions by the railroad In the way of freight rates. The Influence which these railway corporations have acquired in this country is a subject for alarm. It has been my opportunity to sit in the committee room during a number of sessions as a spectator, and I must say that the safety and welfare of this country have depended upon the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway, and other great railway corporations were trying to cut one another's throats. When these great corporations are united as they doubtless will be before long, and united perhaps with the big coal combines of the country, they will have power to make and unmake parliaments. These big corporations do not care for politics, except in so far as one party or the other will serve them best. For these reasons I say that while I believe this commission will give some measure of relief, for one I shall never be satisfied until Panada owns her railroads.

I should be very much inclined myself to despair if the facts were such as stated by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Kendall), and I should feel bound to draw the same conclusion as he does from those facts. The hon. gentleman suggests that if the time ever does arrive, and he imagines it is likely to arrive at some not remote day, when the two great railway corporations, the Canadian Pacific Railway and Grand Trunk Railway, shall unite their interests, they then will have such a controlling power over the parliament of this country that we will be absolutely at their mercy. I feel constrained to express the opinion that even if the time should come, and I am not so sure that that time has not already arrived, when, to all practical intents and purposes, the Canadian Pacific Railway and Grand Trunk Railway are in entire unison in their railway policy, I should be very loath indeed to acknowledge that the people of this country will be unable to defend themselves and to take good

care of their own interests. I think that the railway companies will he sorry to find themselves in antagonism to the people of the country. I think they will not find it to their interest to excite any such conflict, and I believe, Sir, that the managers of these two railways are in their hearts convinced that in such a conflict they are bound to succumb. The people of the country are not in their hands. A few individuals here and there may be largely subject to their influence, but the great body of the people of this Dominion, I am happy to believe, if the time arrives, and they are called upon, are able to go to the polls, and record their votes irrespective of what the two great combined railway corporations may demand. That is my conviction, and I believe that to be the conviction of the majority of the members of this House, and if that were not my conviction, I would despair of the future of this country. . I have followed with all possible interest the discussion that has so far taken place, and I have followed with like interest the discussions which have ensued from time to time, and particularly within the last two months in the newspaper press upon the question of a railway commission, and if one is justified in forming any judgment as to what the state and trend of public opinion is upon this question you would be justified in concluding that the people of Canada are rapidly coming to the opinion that a railway commission would be a very important advance, and that they think its working would be attended with good results. I believe that to be the state of public opinion. I am not in a position to say whether that opinion is founded upon good reason, or whether it is founded upon sufficient ground or not. I am inclined to think that a great many of the most earnest and active and vigorous advocates of a railway commission are led to conclude that it will be a panacea for all of the ills upon grounds which are not sufficient. I have heard, during this discussion, hon. gentlemen specifying their grievances, the grievances of their people, the grievances that are complained of in different sections of the Dominion, and the grievances which they have mentioned, I am bound to say, in my opinion, as far as X have been able to form one, are largely grievances that do not admit of remedy at the hands either of a railway commission, or any other tribunal that can be set up by legislative enactment. Take, for instance, the case mentioned by two or three hon. gentlemen who have spoken. One hon. gentleman, I think it was the hon. member for Bast Grey (Mr. Sproule) mentioned one case, the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) mentioned another, and the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) another. These cases are all very similar. One hon. gentleman said that it was a grievous wrong, and parliament Mr. BLAIR.
ought to remedy such a wrong, that it was possible for the wheat shippers of Chicago to have their wheat carried to the Atlantic seaboard at as low a rate as the farmer at Listowel could have his grain carried to the seaboard. X think reflection will convince anybody that you cannot remedy that state of things, and that if it is a grievance, a grievance it must continue to be. Why ? Because the railway company which is carrying grain from Chicago to the seaboard is obliged to carry it at such rates as will enable it to get the business there, or not carry at all. Our railways which are competing for the traffic from Chicago to the seaboard will carry for rates equal, or very triflingly in excess of the rates to which the hon. gentleman refers, if engaged to carry grain. If the legislature should provide, either by its own direct enactment, or through a commission, that the railway should be forbidden to carry grain from Listowel to the seaboard at the same rates that it charges to carry from Chicago to the seaboard, what would be the result ? The grain would either not be carried from Chicago to the seaboard, or it would not be carried from Listowel to the seaboard. The railway company would make its choice as between the two businesses. Which shall it hold, and which shall it abandon t It would have to determine which was the more profitable. It would have to take into account all the conditions existing, and to say-and the Railway Committee would have to yield to the force of the argument-that the business between Chicago and the seaboard will not be done by this company, or that it will not be done by another company. So that, no injustice is being done to the Listowel farmer. He will not have his grain carried one fraction of a farthing less by reason of the fact that you have prevented the railway company from hauling wheat from Chicago to the seaboard, and he may have to pay an advanced rate because the increased business the company may be getting in its haul from Chicago to the seaboard may enable it to carry grain at a somewhat lower rate from intermediate points. In my opinion it will be impossible that you can so legislate as to prevent business being done under these conditions, so long as railway companies have to confront one another between competitive points. The existing law, the Railway Act, which was framed after due consideration upon this point, I apprehend, contains a clause which distinctly limits the application of the discriminating rule to the case of the carriage of freights between competing points, recognizing that if they did not do that they would be likely to strike a blow at the business of the country which would be vastly more injurious to the general interest and vastly more likely to be productive of the dislocation of the general business of the country

than it would be to omit such a provision from the Act and make an arbitrary rule which shall prescribe that every railway company shall carry every pound of freight hauled on its line at precisely the same comparative figures. X do not think that can be done. That is only one out of many illustrations which can be given of the same character, and which go to show that when you are dealing with questions of this intricate character, of this complicated nature, you cannot work out the ideas that you may think are equitable and just, and at the same time have regard to the demands of business and the conditions which are existing upon the other hand. But, Mr. Speaker, when I say this, I do not pretend to advance it, and I would not be understood as advancing it, as a reason why a commission cannot with great advantage be established by the law of the land. I desired to point that out to show, merely by way of illustration, that the strong reasons which have been urged in this discussion so far by my hon. friends-and they do impress me as being cases of very great grievance-are not reasons upon which it would be wise for parliament to arrive at the conclusion that a railway commission will be able to provide an adequate remedy for these things, and that we will find it a complete answer to all the complaints that are being made.
My hon. friend mentioned a somewhat similar case when he spoke of machinery which was brought from Glasgow and carried all the way from Vancouver at a rate of about one hundred dollars less than the same kind of article was cai'ried from Glasgow to Regina. Is that not a case precisely in point ? There are two or three railways running in competition between the Atlantic seaboard and the Pacific coast. These railways are competing with each other for the business, and in order to secure that business they are obliged to cut under one another, and in doing so they cut their rates down to the lowest possible limit; and so they get the business. Is it any real injury to the people who may be located along that line that the freight is carried by a railway company in this country rather than by a railway company in the United States, and brought in by one of these connecting lines to the Pacific coast ? Would it be an advantage to this country that we should force that traffic over one of the United States lines ? That would be the result, however, if we would say that a railway company cannot impose upon goods which are brought to any point short of the Pacific coast, a rate which, proportionately would be higher than the rate to the coast itself. Hon. gentlemen will see, on a moment's consideration, how full of all sorts of difficulties these questions are. Do not let us jump to the conclusion that a railway commission is going to provide an 28
adequate and complete remedy for all these difficulties, but, taking a moderate view of the question, let us see whether or not there are not things which a railway commission can accomplish which has not been accomplished under the jurisdiction of the Rail way Committee of the Privy Council.
With respect to the action of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council in the past, 1 may fairly claim that it has endeavoured, and with some success, to deal effectually and vigorously with such cases of discrimination under the law as have been brought to its notice. Let it be remembered that all that has been described here to-day as discrimination is not in any sense discrimination under the law. People are apt to give a much wider interpretation to the meaning of the word ' discrimination ' than our present law would warrant, than the word bears in law, under which a railway commission has been established in any other country, or under which a railway commission will be or can be safely established in this country. A railway commission has been established in the mother country. Let us look for a moment how it operates. When I visited England a few years ago I spent a couple of days in the beautiful fruit-growing county of Iient. It is a great strawberry-growing county, and I asked the people about how they forwarded the berries to the London market, the price they paid, and the charges for freight. They told me that for many years they had regarded it as a great grievance that the strawberry-growers and shippers of France, Holland, and Germany were able to send their strawberries to the London market at a lower rate of freight than they themselves had to pay, although they were within from forty to sixty miles of London. I asked an intelligent gentleman with whom I was conversing : Why does not your railway commission apply a remedy, and his answer was ; The railway commission cannot prohibit the shipment from the continent at these low rates ; they cannot control the rates, and our fruit-growers have to fight it out for themselves, and do the best they can. Yet our friends in some parts of Canada think that a similar condition of things can be remedied by the appointment of a railway commission in this country. They cannot afford a remedy in England under the railway commission, or at least they do not do so, and the inference is that, although the railway commission has ample power, they have not found it expedient to interfere, and we may assume that they have very good reasons for their course. We cannot tell in what direction a general dislocation of business would ensue if these matters are thoughtlessly meddled in. and, while relief cannot be afforded in a particular case, or class of cases, it might be attended with serious consequences in other directions, and result in a larger degree of injury being



done. Let me refer again to the Kailway Committee of the Privy Council. Speaking with the best recollection X have of the various questions which have been brought to my attention since I have been Minister of .Railways, I am not aware that there has been any case of discrimination in rates that has not been dealt with by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, if under the law it could deal with it. X remember one or two cases in which we were able to decide that there had been discrimination, and which were dealt witii effectually. The House will remember the complaint as to the arrangement made by the Standard Oil Company with the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway. That complaint was capable of being proven within the law, and when it was proven there was no weakness in the arm of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council to deal with it. We did not hesitate a moment to make up our minds as to what we should do, and the result was that this grievance was abated at once. I do not remember any case in which a complaint was made to us from any part of the country, in which we did not endeavour to get at the facts, and when it appeared that there was discrimination in the sense contemplated by the law, we have applied the remedy. There have been many complaints made to us of alleged discrimination, but there was no discrimination ill them in the sense intended by law, nor was there discrimination in the sense that could be intended by any law we could pass. Hon. gentlemen complain of high rates upon many grounds. I will take the case that was mentioned to-day-the increase of rates between Cranbrook and Lethbridge, or between Lethbridge and Nelson. What is the fact with regard to that case ? The fact is that the rates which are now being imposed by the railway company are not in excess of the rates which they are authorized by law to impose, under the schedule which was fixed by the Governor in Council, with the best information at our disposal. It is true, there was a raise in the rate not very long since; but that raise occurred in this way. There was a reduction previously ; or, when the rate was first fixed, it was away below the schedule. For some reason or other, the companies concerned felt that these rates were too low, and they raised them ; but they did not raise them beyond or up to the schedule of rates allowed them by law, or when the tariff was submitted to and approved by the Governor in Council. It does not follow by any means that because we approve of a schedule of rates, the railway companies will always or to any great degree maintain their rates up to that schedule. That is the maximum. We have to fix a maximum. It is the only way in which rates could be fixed by us or by a railway commission. We cannot Mr. BLAIR.
fix a rate to-day on this railway for a part of Its line, and another rate tomorrow for another part of its line. We have to make a general rate for a district or area of country, arriving as well as we can at a conclusion as to what would be a fair and reasonable maximum rate to allow, from the best information we can gather, considering the different conditions of the different belts or areas. We have to consider the cost of operating the line. We do not often consider the question of the cost of building the line or the extent to which bonds have been issued. These are not the things we have in our minds ; but we have thought that we could best arrive at fair results with regard to a tariff of rates by comparison with other roads operating under like conditions, in other countries it may be, or in our own. For instance, when we were determining what we would approve as the maximum scale for the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, we took pains to ascertain what were the schedules allowed and in operation upon the lines to the south of the boundary traversing the same description of country as our own ; and I will state to the House now that after a careful comparison of the rates, local and through, which were fixed by the authorities in the different states and territories to the south of the boundary line, we fixed as the maximum a lower schedule of rates upon the Canadian Pacific Railway traversing the Crow's Nest Pass than were allowed on those other railways. In every single instance, I think, we fixed lower rates in respect to all the classifications of goods and in respect to all the distances. At all events, we did so in the great majority of cases. So that it is not fair to say, and it cannot be said with a knowledge of the facts, that the schedules upon the Crow's Nest Pass Railway are higher than the schedules upon the other roads which are traversing east and west, south of the boundary line.
I have no doubt that while these maximum schedules are as they are, there are reasons why some of the railways to the south, perhaps all of them, may issue their tariffs upon a lower scale than the maximum. I have no doubt that they do it just as we do it. Possibly they may under some particular circumstances make some of their classifications lower and some of their distances lower. But we cannot by any possibility avoid that, and no tribunal, no railway commission, could reach a general conclusion as to what ought to be a fair maximum rate, in respect to all those classifications and in respect to distances, in any other way than the result was arrived at by the Governor in Council. It is not a thing which is capable of mathematical demonstration. There is no way in which we can figure out what would be absolutely right, what the business ought to stand, or what the business would not stand, what the conditions of the people will enable them to pay, or

what the conditions of the people in a locality will not enable them to pay. We cannot reach these results by any precise scientific method. We have to do it in a crude way, by comparison with other railways, and railways whose applications are before us. When you come to examine, therefore, into the complaints which are so frequently made in the public press, as a matter of fact many of them will be found to be based, in the first place, upon insufficient information, and in the next place, upon the drawing of improper inferences from information which they may accurately have.
But, all the same, I frankly acknowledge, as I stated a moment ago, that there are strong reasons why it would be well for us to try the experiment of a railway commission. It is not possible for us to introduce a Bill for that purpose at the present session. I may frankly confess that if any culpability attaches for the non-presentation of a Bill of that kind at the present session, I would be in duty bound to assume the largest measure of responsibility upon myself. I want to disabuse the mind of my hon. friend from Bast Grey (Mr. Sproule) when he suggests, not probably intending to do anybody any injustice, that my inclination may perhaps be all right, but that 1 find myself overborne or prevented by the influence of others, or perhaps by my colleagues. I want to say to the House that so far as I have any means of judging, my colleagues are as well disposed as I am to favour tile experiment of a railway commission, and I confidently believe that it will be one way of convincing the public mind that there are difficulties in the way of handling these questions which are not of a political character, which do not take their rise from any political influence or pressure, but which are necessarily incident to the transaction of a business that has grown to enormous proportions during recent years, which it is an immensely complicated problem to solve. I do not say that the railway commissions in the United States have not done good work, but they have fallen very far short of the expectations which were formed for them. I do not say that the railway commission in England has not done good work, but I do say that it has absolutely failed to meet the expectations which were held out respecting it, and there is a strong agitation in that country against its continuance.
During the course of this discussion, some of our friends have pointed out a few matters which they think might fairly come within the scope of such commission. The hon. gentleman from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) thought that the charter-mongers perhaps might be sent adrift if a railway commission were established, and that the duty might well be imposed upon the commission of investigating into the sufficiency of all applications to parliament for railway 28J
charters, and reporting the conditions upon which these charters should be granted, and the extent of bonding privileges that should be conceded. I hardly think that parliament would be willing to denude itself entirely of the power of granting railway Charters. We are supposed to make some inquiry into these applications. We are in tlie habit of inquiring into the necessity for the railway asked for and of imposing restrictions against the excessive issue of bonds. It is not difficult for any member of parliament to procure information as to tlie reasonable necessity of constructing a railway in any section of our country, nor is it difficult to get information as to the probable cost, in a general way, and we usually have that information furnished us. When there is any conflict as to the granting of a charter, the subject is pretty thoroughly discussed, and we have ample means of forming a judgment as to whether the charter should be granted or refused. I question, therefore, whether it would be well for parliament to refuse to retain in its hands to the fullest extent the right of granting these applications made from time to time. The question of railway construction is not one which has ceased to be, by any means, a live question. I believe that we are only entering upon the work of railway construction in Canada. Railways are just as necessary as highways. You will have to increase your railways in our great western country, ten-fold, twentyfold, perhaps one hundred-fold, before you get that country developed. We are, in fact, only upon the threshold of the opening up and proper development of our great western inheritance. Bet us not forget that the people in these different localities are impressed to a degree that we perhaps, in this section of the country, can hardly realize, with the importance of having railways laid down in their midst. These railways are an absolute and vital necessity to the filling up of this country. And when the people are crying out for railways, I do not think it would be wise policy for parliament to place undue obstacles in the way of chartering these roads.
The same experience will be undergone in the west that we have had in the east. We will find the people there crying out almost in despair for the construction of railways in every section of the country, giving, and themselves supplicating their municipalities to help, calling upon the provincial legislatures to contribute, and also upon the Dominion parliament to eome to their rescue. They do so because railways are to them a paramount necessity, and because there is no reasonable amount of debt that they would not feel justified in incurring in order to secure railway construction in their midst. Therefore, we in this part of the country ought not to be any less generous in our treatment of applications for rail-

way assistance in these unopened sections of our great west, than we have been in the past when dealing with applications for railways nearer the great centres and in the older provinces of Canada. We must not shut our eyes to the growing necessities of that country ; we cannot refuse to give it liberal treatment. If we should, we would be adopting an unwise policy, and one which will be attended with much more serious results than even going a little to the extreme the other way.
I do not think I would be justified in dwelling any longer on this question. I did not intend speaking at such length, but I wish to make one concluding remark. The Bill to establish a railway commission cannot be introduced this session. I stated in the House last year that I hoped at an early date to be able to introduce such a measure, but at that time I did not sufficiently carry in mind the fact that as soon as parliament was over, we would be plunged into the engrossing occupation of a general election. That absorbed pretty well all the time and attention which would have [DOT]been possible for me to give to any other subject, and from that time down, there has not been any opportunity open to me of taking the subject up and considering and examining it as it must necessarily be considered, weighed and examined, if a Bill was to come up for consideration of parliament in such a form as it ought to come before receiving the sanction of this legislature.
In the meantime, and while we are waiting for another session, we are considering now whether it might not be to advantage that we should set somebody to work who, without our incurring a very large expense, might become possessed, by inquiry upon the spot, of the real facts and the full extent of the grievances which may be remediable, and which are finding expression in the public press and on the floor of this House. Such an investigation would be attended, I think, with two great results-it would put us in a position, when we finally draft our measure, to know, at all events, the nature of the difficulties which, so far as it is possible to do so, we hope to be able to surmount; and it would, at the same time, enable us to find whether or not there are at the moment existing in these localities any grievances which the Railway Committee itself could deal with and deal with promptly, before we should have time to introduce and pass a law dealing with this subject. That is the feeling and disposition of the government. My own personal desire, Mr. Speaker, is that we should grapple with the question-a question necessarily of great importance, and one that is engaging largely the attention of the general public throughout the whole of Canada- and grapple with it vigorously. Let it strike where it may, so far as any improper Mr. BLAIR.
railway interest is concerned. Railway interest we must consider, but improper, unreasonable railway interest we are not justified in considering. And when I say that this is my own feeling, I am bound to say, as a matter of justice to every one of my colleagues, that I believe, from what has occurred and from the opinions thev have expressed, and from what they have said to me, that they are as deeply sensible of the importance of our meeting, as fully as possible, the complaints which are being made throughout the country, and are as strongly disposed as I am myself to aid in any measure which will ensure an adequate and efficient remedy.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext:
In closing this debate, I would like to take a few moments to answer some of the statements made by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, and also statements made by the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair). If I understand the argument of the Minister of Railways, it amounts simply to this-that without competition, the people can get no relief, for, in discussing the point brought up by the hon. gentleman from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) with reference to the haul of grain from Chicago as compared with the charge from Listowel, Ont., I understood him to say that competition would force the railway companies to give a. lower rate from Chicago than from Listowel. Now, as I have said, we in the North-west Territories live at a distance from the head of ocean navigation, and we had hoped for some relief from the rate charged on our grain from the grain fields of the west to the head of navigation, and I cited this afternoon the fact that we were paying 8f cents per bushel for hauling our grain from Winnipeg, 448 miles, as against 4J cents paid by the people, no matter who they are, who have their grain hauled a thousand miles, in round numbers, to Montreal, on the lakes, and the Canada Atlantic. So, I think we had a right to claim some relief. My hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) says that the Canadian Pacific Railway, in the kindness of their hearts, have offered to reduce the rates on grain to the lakes to 4 cents a bushel, provided the people of Manitoba will deal with them instead of dealing with a competing line, the Canada Northern. In view of this fact, I think the people of the west may justly claim that the government should step in and give them some relief. It seems to me a sad thing if the government cannot do this. If we must get competing lines in order to secure cheaper freight rates, it is a good thing for the people to know that fact. But, I submit that if one railway can do all the work under proper supervision and control, it would be better to have one railway than two ; for, if they have one railway, it can do the work for less than two railways can do it for when it is divided between them.

Of course, we do not expect that a railway commission would be a panacea for all the ills that flesh is heir to. We never advanced that idea. But we think that with a properly constituted railway commission we could get relief from some grievances. I showed this afternoon that the local rates on coal oil between Petrolia and Winnipeg, and Winnipeg and Prince Albert, are together 11 cents less than the through rate from Petrolia to Prince Albert. That is a grievance that a railway commission could deal with. Other questions also would arise. We have had any number of grievances in the North-west. For instance, for two or three sessions here, a good deal of time was taken up in discussing the Elevator Bill, and trying to get relief for the people in the handling of their grain. If we had had a properly constituted railway commission, the question could have been dealt with by that commission without troubling this House. Another point was that referred to by my kon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) in connection with the locating of a station. We do not want to be at the mercy of a railway corporation, because a big corporation like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company can make or break towns. If we propose to tax them and they do not want to pay the taxes, they can remove the station to some other place and build a town there. The case referred to by the hon. member for Alberta was that of Pincher Creek. A branch of the Crow's Nest line, passed within two miles of Pincher Creek. The people of the town petitioned the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to place their station at the nearest point to the town. The railway company replied that on account of a grade or something, it was impossible for them to do so. So they put the station about two miles up the track, or about four miles from the town. Then the people applied to the government, I suppose to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, that my hon. friend from South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) thinks is so much better and more suitable to the requirements of the country than a railway commission, but the reply of that body was that nothing could be done. But, lo and behold, a short time after, the Canadian Pacific Railway wrote and wired to the people of Pincher Creek, telling them they would place their station on the very spot where the people asked them to build it in the first place, and would do it without money and without price, though, in the first instance, the people offered a certain sum if they would place it there. A question of that kind could be settled by a properly constituted railway commission if we had one.
Now, I want to point out another fact to the Minister of Railways and Canals. In the town in which I live we have a salt deposit, and we would not have to go more than 250 miles east with our salt in order to
be able to develop quite an industry in that town; but we cannot do it simply on account of the freight rates. We find the people in Goderich load their salt as ballast on boats going across the lakes, and get such low rates from the Canadian Pacific Railway, that they can place their salt down in competition to us, and drive us out of our own markets. I claim that is a grievance.
Now, I find in comparing the rates between Buffalo and New York over the New York Central, and it is about the same distance as from Winnipeg to the great lakes, that the shippers over that road have to pay something like 3 cents a bushel as compared with the 8 2-5 cents per bushel that we pay for the same distance in the west. I have shown this afternoon that they charge in the town of Prince Albert, in which I live, more for hauling stuff 609 miles, than they charge the people of Calgary for hauling 840 miles. I do not see where the long haul comes in there. If they hauled for the people of Calgary for the same price as the people of Prince Albert, then there might be some force in the argument of the Minister of Railways and Canals; but when they charge us 3 and 4 cents per 100 pounds more for carrying freight a shorter distance than they charge the people of Calgary, I think we have a grievance.
I want now to refer to the speech of the hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale). That hon. gentleman appears to me to be a venerable Rip Van Winkle. He appears to have been asleep for the last 15 or 20 years and to have just wakened up; because he has treated us this afternoon to a tale of ancient history about the Grand Trunk Railway. He tells up that the Grand Trunk Railway, with all the money that had been invested in it, much of which he says was invested by widows and orphans, had never paid more than 11 cents per mile on the money invested. I wish he had gone further and told us how much money had been invested in the road. I think it would be found that the road is bonded to about double what it is worth. As was said by the hon. member for Grey, the people should not be called upon to pay interest on double what a railroad is worth, but only upon the exact amount taken in the first place to build the road. Is it right that the people of Alberta should be called upon to pay interest on 5 million dollars, when their road only cost 3 millions by the statement of the company In the blue-books ? I do not think that is a fair proposition. Therefore, I say it is time some steps should be taken by the government; and if we cannot get relief by a railroad commission, then we will have to go a step further, and the government will have to take control of the roads as they have done in Australia and other countries.
Book at the bearing of this question on the North-west Territories. If we are ever to get that country opened up and developed,

its mineral resources witli its wealth of timber and fisheries and agricultural lands, we must have some relief from railroad oppression. We will not get people to come into that country otherwise. A pioneer who is an intelligent man is sent in by his fellow-farmers to look out locations, and the first thing that man will do is to inquire what he will have to pay for hauling his produce to market. When be is told that be will bave to pay 8 2-5 cents a bushel for hauling his grain 448 miles, be will compare that rate with what the people have to pay in the United States, with what they bave to pay in Australia and other countries, in the Argentine Republic and in Brazil, and that man will go somewhere else to seek a location on account of the exorbitant freight rates.
I am sorry the Minister of Railways thinks we cannot get a measure of relief from this commission. I think, however, it would be well to give the experiment a trial. I have studied the report of the railway commission in the United States, and I find that outside of the question of freight rates altogether they have been a great advantage. I do not suppose a railway commission would cost more than $40,000 or $50,000 a year, not too big a sum for a country growing like this. There are a hundred ways in which it could be a benefit to the people. Take, for instance, a poor farmer in the west whose cow or horse is killed on the railroad track. He makes an appeal to the railroad corporation for compensation, and if they feel disposed in the kindness of their heart, they will give him something for it, but in case they refuse to pay him he is at their mercy, and can do nothing, because they will carry the case from court to court, and finally to the Privy Council, and the poor man will be ruined. If you had a properly constituted railroad commission that poor man could carry his case before them, they would investigate it, and if they found that he had a just case, they would order the corporation to settle with him, and if they refused to do so they would have the government to deal with instead of that private individual.
The hon. member for Norfolk said this afternoon that the Grand Trunk Railway had not paid more than 11 per cent on the money that had been invested. And what is the reason ? Because the money has been wasted. There is a case in point, an object lesson for any gentleman who has passed over the road between this town and Toronto. I have looked out of the window and seen about 50 miles of railroad graded upon which there had never been a tie or a piece of iron laid. That road cost about $600,000 of the money of these poor widows and orphans the hon. gentleman was talking about. If there had been a properly constituted railway commission existing in this country at that time, that money never would have Mr. DAVIS.
been wasted, because a charter would never have been granted.
The Minister of Railways thinks that parliament would be denuding itself of its powers by placing the control in the hands of a railroad commission. I never made a proposition of that kind. What I said was that when an application was made to this House, and that application was handed over to a railroad commission for them to examine into the facts and report back to this House, on that report parliament would be in a position to deal intelligently with the question. That is what I said. With all due respect for the members of the Railway Committee, I do not think that they are at all times seized with all the information that they should possess. Some gentleman comes there with a beautiful map and places it on the wall and shows the point where the road is going to, and perhaps it does not go within a hundred miles of the point shown on the map. That is about all the information they get, and we pass these charters. I would like to know how many bogus and straw charters there are in this country at the present time. You have them all over the North-west Territories; you have railroads running to Hudson Bay and Timbuctoo, and everywhere else, on which there has never been a shovelful of mud turned, and never will be. But these people come back to parliament and ask for an extension of time so that they may be able to keep this charter until something turns up so that they can turn it into money; or perhaps under a government that is a little soft in that respect they may be able to get a subsidy, and then they will have something to sell. I say if a properly constituted commission was in existence, we would not be troubled with this charter-mongering. We have suffered from that in the west.
Take- the case mentioned by the hon. member for Grey this afternoon, the Great North-west Central. That charter was granted some twenty years ago, it bore a land grant of 6,400 acres per mile, they built 50 miles, and they never built any more until forced by this House two or three years ago to build 20 miles, and that is all that they have ever done. Still the people have settled 100 miles ahead of that line, waiting for relief, and nothing is being done. I hope the government will see its way clear at least to try the experiment of appointing this railway commission. The Minister of Railways says there is a disposition in England to do away with the commission. But, we find in the United States for the last 25 years they have been in existence, and I am sure that the people in that country are too intelligent to keep anything of that kind in existence if it was of no benefit to the people.
We find that the reports of every state that has a commission are placed before

the country, and you can see exactly what they are doing. I would advise all the hon. members of this House to take the trouble to read these reports, and, as the hon. member for Bast Grey (Mr. Sproule) said this afternoon, they would find from them that a great deal of benefit had accrued to the people. I am sure that when the hon. member for South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) shuffles off this mortal coil the people of the North-west Territories will erect a monument to his memory, because he has always exerted his influence, so strongly in committee and out of committee in their interests. From a political standpoint, 1 would like if the hon. gentleman would come out through the North-west Territories and express himself as he has done in this House this afternoon. It would be the best thing that could happen for the Liberal party. I believe it would do them more good even than the trip of the late leader of the opposition (Sir Charles Tupper), because, in place of having six seats in the entire country west of Winnipeg after the elections as is now the case, the opposition would then have none. I hope the government will, in the near future, see their way clear to do something in the way of trying to give the settlers, not only in the North-west Territories, but of other parts of the Dominion, the remedy that is needed by appointing a railway commission.

Mr. Speaker, before the question is put, I would like to say a word. So far as this motion is concerned it does not seem to point to anything very definite. The motion is :
That the public interests demand that the railway companies of Canada should, at the earliest moment, be brought under control of a board of railway c mmissioners, clothed with full power to enforce the provisions of the Railway Act.
Well, the Railway Act is enforced to some extent by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, and possibly to some extent by the courts, and it is occasionally difficult to find out whether you are to go to the court or the Railway Committee of the Privy Council with a particular matter. So far as that uncertainty or difficulty is concerned, it seems to me that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) may very well devote his attention to it, and amend the Railway Act for the purpose of making that clear. I had occasion some time ago to examine the Railway Act with respect to a difficulty between two railways, and I found a great deal of legal difficulty in knowing whether or not you should go to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council or to the court. That is a subject which might very well be dealt with by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals in framing legislation. As to the project of transferring the power to enforce the
provisions of the Railway Act, so far as they are enforceable by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, to a railway commission, that depends to some extent on the question as to whether the Railway Committee of the Privy Council is found to be an efficient body for the purpose for which it was intended. There may be something in the suggestion which has been made, I think, by the hon. mover of this motion (Mr. Davis), with respect to the want of time on the part of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council to deal with these matters, but, on the other hand, we have the assurance upon which, no doubt, we may rely, of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, that every case which has been brought before the Railway Committee of the Privy Council has been dealt with by that body. I understand the hon. gentleman to give that assurance to the House.
Yes, that is so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The rest of the motion is clothed in terms almost as delightfully vague as those in which the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals expressed his intentions in regard to this commission in the future.
And to prescribe and enforce the observance of such regulations as may be necessary in the public interest.
I think almost every hon. gentleman In this House may be permitted to support the principle of this resolution in regard to that, but, possibly, when we came to decide among ourselves as to what regulations were in the public interest, there would be a good deal of divergence among hon. members on one side or the other as to what these regulations should be. However, so far as that particular portion of it is concerned, it is worded in such a delightfully vague manner, that I am sure there is hardly an hon. gentleman in this House who will have the heart to say a word against it.
I agree with the hon. gentlemen in this House who have doubted whether it is possible by means of a railway commission, or by any legislation, to bring to an end the evils and the complaints in respect to railway transportation. So far as a railway commission is concerned the words in this resolution mean nothing at all. The question is : What powers are you going to give the commission ? Are you going to give it merely advisory powers, as in Massachusetts, or the power of a court, as in other states ? What do you mean by a railway commission ? That is the thing you must decide in the first instance, and the House can not be prepared to pass upon the subject intelligently upon any such vague resolution as this. You must first

bring down a measure, and say whether you are going to have an advisory commission or to give it the power of a court, and you must reasonably define all its powers, before we can intelligently discuss it. It does not seem to me that there is really anything very definite in this resolution. Undoubtedly a railway commission will not necessarily bring to an end the evils which have been spoken of here to-night. That is perfectly plain from what the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has told us, and from what other hon. gentlemen have told us in regard to the state of affairs in England to-day. If a railway commission would bring all these evils to an end, the farmers of Waies would not be complaining that it costs them more to carry their produce to London than it costs the farmers of Ontario to carry their produce to London. I do not suppose it is possible to cure a matter of that kind by any legislation. As the hon. Minister of. Railways and Canals has pointed out, this is a very complex question. You have to take into consideration competing lines, you have to take into consideration the lines which compete by water and the lines which compete partly by land and partly by water. You cannot cure all of these matters by appointing a railway commission and passing Acts of parliament. The great complexity of business transactions makes it absolutely impossible to deal with matters of this kind to the satisfaction of every one, and possibly makes it necessary that incongruities of this kind should sometimes exist.
I do sympathize with the remarks of the hon. mover of this resolution respecting the granting of what he calls straw charters and the giving of enormously large bonding powers to railway companies.
