I do not believe that railway charters, or any other charters in this country, should be made the subject of speculation, and I also recognize the fact that this is an evil which may not be very easy to deal with. I have tried to think out in my own mind some remedy for an evil of that kind, and I may say that I have not completely satisfied my own mind as to what would be the best mode in which to deal with it. It occurred to me that possibly if we required from the promoters of every new railway company the making of a deposit which would guarantee good faith and an intention on the part of the people who received the charter that they intended to build the railway, good might result, but possibly the only effect of that would be that when they came to sell the charter they would charge a higher price from the persons to whom they sold it. I do not at all feel sure as to what the proper remedy is, although I entirely agree with the suggestions of those who believe that some remedy should be found. Bonding powers should correspond *with the cost of the road in some reasonable Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
degree. There are two reasons amongst others for that. The first thing that occurs to me is that by giving too large bonding powers you may be leading into a trap unwary in* vestors, and in the next place, although the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals assures us that the question of the amount of bonds, or the question of the amount of stock does not enter at all into the consideration of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council when dealing with rates, nevertheless we know that these things are put forward in the public press, if they are not put forward any place else. That is an additional reason why the bonding power should be carefully guarded, and I take it that the Minister of Railways is of tlie opinion that these should not be unduly extended. I hardly thought that the minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) gave sufficient weight to what was suggested by the hon. member from Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall). What the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendall) said was that if all or the majority of the great railways of Canada combined in a vast trust with persons who became possessed of enormous interests in connection with the coal and iron aud other industries of the country, there might be fear in the future. I do not think the hon. member intended to suggest, nor do I intend to suggest, that there is any present or immediate danger in Canada of that kind. I am not suggesting that, but we know that so far back as in 1880 in the United States it was publicly charged that great trusts did exercise a very pronounced influence upon legislatures. In fact the statement made by responsible persons went very much further than I have indicated. I am only suggesting, in passing, that possibly what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendall) said might require a little more serious consideration than the Minister of Railways was disposed to give it upon his attention being first directed to it. It seems to me that in its present form the resolution is so extremely vague as not to commit the House to anything beyond the proposition that a railway commission could do the work of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council better than the work is being done by that body. I am not sufficiently familiar with the way in which the Railway Committee of the Privy Council discharges its duty to say whether that is the case or not, but if we take, as we are bound to take, the statement of the Minister of Railways on that point, it seems to me that that particular portion of the motion hardly seems to be justified by anything that has been advanced in support of it.

OSLEIt (West Toronto). There is just one point to which I would draw the attention of the House, because it may give some indication of the wild statements that have been made by some hon. gentlemen in this discussion. The hon. gentleman from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) has referred to the Regina and Long Lake Railway. If he

will refer to the railway returns he will find that the gross earnings of that railway company for the last year amounted to $100,702, and the working expenses amounted to $115,500, so that the road was operated in favour of the country through which it passes and In favour of that hon. gentleman's constituency at a direct loss of $15,000. If the road had been built for nothing-as far as the country is concerned it was built for nothing-it has paid its bondholders or shareholders not one dollar interest, and it is being operated now at a loss. It has been operated at a loss since the day it was opened. It was a very unfortunate thing to build a road in such a country, but the origin of that road was because the government wanted to build a railway into the Prince Albert district after the rebellion. The reports in the department at that time showed that the land through which the railway ran was supposed to be good land, but it has turned out that the land is barren land until you get near Prince Albert. I can see no future to the road, and unless some change takes place there is only one thing that can happen to it, and that is that the road must be closed up.
It should never have been built.

Quite right, it should never have been built; but it cannot be continued to be run at a loss and the question of the exorbitant charges have nothing to do with the working of that road, or with the rates which may be charged upon it.
Motion (Mr. Davis) agreed to.

subtopic: VIRDEN, QTT'APPEDLE, REGINA AND MOOSEJAW TOWN SITES.
VIRDEN, QTT'APPEDLE, REGINA AND MOOSEJAW TOWN SITES.
speechtext:
OSLER (West Toronto) moved for :
Return of a certain report presented to the Department of the Interior by the commissioners appointed on June 19th last to audit all accounts and investigate and report upon all matters connected with the administration and sale by trustees of the town sites of Virden, Qu'Appelle, Regina and Moosejaw.
He said : I wish to make a few remarks on this motion, because perhaps there are very few hon. gentlemen in the House who are aware what this Town Site Trust is. In 1882 the Canadian North-west Land Co. bought about two million acres from the Canadian Pacific Railway, and with that they bought a half-interest in the town sites from the western boundary of Manitoba to the boundary of British Columbia. For that they paid at the rate of one-half dollar an acre extra, or nearly a million dollars. The government asked that they should be interested in certain town sites along that district, and consequently the government obtained a half-interest in four town sites, Regina, Virden, Qu'Appelle and Moosejaw.
Trustees were appointed to administer the town sites, and the trustees were Lord Strathcona, Mr. R. B. Angus, Mr. Scarth and Mr. Osier. Those trustees administered the town sites and they sold altogether about a million dollars worth of lots. They administered under an agreement with the government, and I think they acted strictly under the terms of that agreement. In June last the government appointed a commission to inquire and report on these town sites. The report was brought in and it was handed to two or three of tjie government newspapers, and in January last these papers, the Globe especially, commented upon that report. The Globe headed its article :
Money Flew Fast In the Good Old Tory Days- Discoveries made by the North-west Townsites Commission-Fleecing the Government-How Mr. T. M. Daly made a handsome price for land in which he had no rights-Mr. Davin's loan- How the Government was made to pay for Mr. Davin's Newspaper Plant-Heavy Refunds to Speculators, some of them represented by trustees-Large sums paid out in Unauthorized Salaries-Cash Statement-Government out about $50,000-Names of Witnesses called before Commission-Mr. Osier Objects, to Testifying-Text of the Report of the Commissioners.
Now, the Globe makes a summary of the report, the main points of which are : That Mr. Daly received $6,400 for a section of land in Virden which had really belonged to the government. The renting and final purchasing of the building of the trustees by the government at an exorbitant price. The trustees lending the money to Mr. Davin to start a newspaper. The trustees refunding various sums to persons who had bought for speculative purposes ; the government charged improperly for many town sites; and that Mr. Osier, Mr. Scarth and others drew large sums of money in salaries and otherwise. Now, the land which the government contributed toward those town sites realized in the actual sale not much more than one-third of the whole amount; that is to say, the land contributed by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the other parties was very much more valuable.
I have a report here by Mr. Hamilton, the land commissioner, and Mr. Ogden, the auditor and comptroller of the Canadian Pacific Railway, in which they answer these charges as they are made. As regards the Virden town site, Mr. Daly had a claim upon it, and it was necessary to secure that claim at once, or the sale of the lots would have been lost; the station and town site would have been located elsewhere :
The agreement, for the administration of the town sites states the amount of land to be contributed by each party. In the case of Virden, the entire quantity is to be contributed by the government. There is nothing unusual in this, as at that time any party owning land was very willing to give all the land to have a station and a town site located, retaining a half interest in the net proceeds of sale of lots in the town. The commissioners find that Mr. COMMONS
Daly had rights on the south half of the section until he dismissed the entry, which was probably done when he was paid $6,400. The government contributed the section and the $6,400 was paid to clear the title. The whole amount should have been charged to the government instead of one-half.
With regaitl to Mr. Davin. At that time I had not the pleasure of knowing Mr. Davin personally ; but the loan to him was made for the purpose of establishing a newspaper in the new government town

a very wise and necessary expenditure. I think that even notv the government feel that it is necessary in some cases to contribute to the support of newspapers. I notice in a return that one newspaper published in the largest city of Canada, receives in pap or in contributions $40,000 or $50,000. The amount in question was contributed quite properly, and was an investment which paid, because advertising had to be done ; and while the newspaper was apparently carried on at a loss, Mr. Davin's covenants were released, when the property had to be taken back by the trustees, which was a very proper thing to do. Certain money was refunded at Regina, after full consideration and investigation, because very large taxes were running up there, and that had to be done in the interest of all parties.
It is claimed that certain salaries were paid to Mr. Scarth, Mr. Campbell, and others as extra clerks. These salaries were perfectly proper, and were chargeable to the trustees and the government. The Canadian Pacific Railway in the same case paid a very much larger sum for salaries than was charged to the government. The trustees, X may say, in connection with the administration of these town sites, have never personally drawn one dollar. Report says that X drew a certain amount-$500. I did draw an amount-I think it was $1,200. I drew that money when the office was being removed and certain clerks were being discharged. I saw no other way of bonusing those men ; and, as I was entitled to remuneration as a trustee, I drew a certain insignificant amount for that purpose. The administration of this trust, amounting to $1,000,000, has been carried on without the expense of one dollar charged by the trustees to the government; but if they appealed to a court in Ontario to-day, those trustees would be awarded a remuneration of at least $50,000 for their work. Thousands of deeds and thousands of agreements have been signed. A gratuity was paid to Mr. Gosling, who, when the business was large, was employed as the chief accountant. The business fell off, and naturally he was paid a comparatively small sum on leaving the trustees. Now, I make the statement that from first to last there has never been a trust in Canada administered so faithfully, so squarely, so thoroughly, for the benefit of all concerned.

subtopic: VIRDEN, QTT'APPEDLE, REGINA AND MOOSEJAW TOWN SITES.
speechtext:
It is charged further that there were certain rebates made to parties who purchased town lots. That is quite true. Rebates were made to a great many town lot purchasers, amoung others to a Scottish company. Mr. Scarth was connected with that company. It had spent hundreds of thousands of pounds, I think, in the development of north-west interest. It had established a stock farm on the Manitoba and Northwestern Railway, and had brought out high-class cattle, the result being that from along that line to-day probably the finest cattle that are brough from the North-west come. Too much credit cannot be given to the enterprise of that company. Unfortunately, the venture proved a failure. The trustees, with the consent of the government, refunded to that company $30,000 or $40,000 of the money which they had expended in town lots in Regina. So far for being blamed for that, I say the trustees are entitled to every credit.
I can understand that probably it was a proper thing for the government to have a report made on this subject, although every year audited statements were submitted to the government, approved and accepted by the government, and the money due to the government was paid over. But this report was made, and was handed out to one or two government newspapers, apparently for the purpose of having those newspapers comment upon two or three gentlemen connected with that trusteeship. They singled out one of the trustees, who has been for a number of years a government official. Perhaps his place was wanted, and a little excuse was necessary. The chief attack, however, has apparently been made upon myself. The report closes with a statement that Mr. Osier objected to testify. I did object to testify, but under these circumstances. The two commissioners came into my office one morning with a shorthand reporter, their secretary. They began asking me questions concerning this town site in 1882, before I had anything to do with it. I was not a trustee until nearly a year and a half after that. They began to ask me questions about financial matters, about payments that took place eighteen years ago, and I replied that I was quite unprepared from memory to talk about such transactions. The books had been taken from Toronto seventeen years ago, I think, and I did not see them after they had gone to Winnipeg, and concerning the transactions referred to, I knew nothing personally. I told those commissioners that perhaps I could tell them where and how they could get information, but if they were going to examine me on matters that occurred nearly twenty years ago-matters connected with figures-I refused to testify without having the books sent down from the North-west. In that refusal, I think I was perfectly justified.

I do not think that the commissioners were justified in completing their report by emphasizing, as they did, the fact that Mr. Osier was the only one who refused to give evidence. The only inference that can be drawn, as far as I can see, is that the government expected to find some serious irregularities in the administration of that town trust, and the commissioners found that there were no irregularities. The report was given out to two or three newspapers, which made this severe attack. As soon as the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is the only company having anything to do with the government, was apprised of this report, it asked the government for a copy of the evidence. This report was published in the Globe on the 5th of January, 1901. But up to this date, the government have failed to comply with that request. These two commissioners, acting by themselves, taking what they saw fit to take, looking at the books as they liked, brought in an account showing that the trustees are liable to the government for $40,000, and asked them to put that to the credit of the government.

subtopic: VIRDEN, QTT'APPEDLE, REGINA AND MOOSEJAW TOWN SITES.
speechtext: Who were the commissioners ?

subtopic: VIRDEN, QTT'APPEDLE, REGINA AND MOOSEJAW TOWN SITES.
speechtext:
Mr. Smart and Mr. E. F. Stephenson. The Canadian Pacific Railway is directly responsible to the government for the administration of that trust. These trustees were accepted by the government, but the Canadian Pacific Railway was the original trustee, and assumed all liability for the share of the government's money that would accrue. Application was made to the government for this evidence, so that a more complete answer might be given, but that evidence has not yet been furnished. The Canadian Pacific Railway then asked that the government refer the accounts to a commission or to a court, and the government simply wrote saying : We do not propose to take further action in this matter ; place this money to our credit.
The trustees, one and all, for a long time have desired to resign. They wish to have this trust divided and be no longer partners with the government. They applied to the government to have this done, and the government at one time accepted the suggestion, but since then the government have changed their minds, and only on the 27th February last they wrote to Mr. Hamilton, the land commissioner :
Dear Mr. Hamilton,-I have yours of the 23rd inst., with reference to a division of the remaining lots of the towns of Virden and Qu'Appellc-, Regina and Moosejaw. In reply, would say that it is not thought advisable to make a division at the present time.
This is a report of the commissioners on the four trustees, who each assumed equal responsibility-Lord Strathcona, R. B. Angus, W. B. Scarth, E. B. Osier-and it casts a slur upon the administration of those gentlemen. Yet, in the report, from end to end, there is not a single item, which is not a credit to the administration of that trust from the beginning to the end. There is not a single item or transaction which has not been approved by the government. There is not a single item or transaction, in the whole administration of that trust for nearly twenty years, which does not reflect credit on the ability, honesty, and forethought of the trustees. Those trustees have administered that trust for themselves, for the North Western Land Co., and for the government, the government receiving half of the net proceeds. They have sold in that time within a few dollars of $1,000,000 of town lots at prices running from $10 up to several thousand. Of course a good many of those sales had eventually to be cancelled after the boom burst and the purchasers could not meet their payments. The trustees have paid the government some $200,000 for its half-interest, when the real interest of the government in the land sold was only $132,000.
There is one other complaint made by the commissioners which I have overlooked. They say that the Canadian Pacific Railway took to itself some acres of land at $3 an acre, but the only objection that could be raised to that is that the Canadian Pacific Railway should have paid anything, because the agreement provides that both the government and the Canadian Pacific Railway shall have all the land required for railway or government purposes free.
I do not propose to comment upon this report. If I were to express myself as I feel, I am afraid I should be called to order very suddenly and sharply by the Speaker. But I cannot understand how such a report came to be issued. I cannot understand how the government could have asked to have such a report made, or to have that report issued exclusively in two or three partisan journals, with the headings outlined and whom to attack marked out, and then have refused to give at once a copy of the evidence. I cannot understand how the government should refuse to dissolve a partnership, after bringing in a report which is interpreted by the newspapers to mean that these trustees have administered wrongfully that trust. Why the government should have refused absolutely to dissolve the trust and allow the trustees to withdraw from the administration is something I cannot understand. Who instigated this report, I do not know. I only know that it was issued apparently for the purpose of doing harm and injury, and issued in such a way as to try and mislead the public and cast a slur upon the trustees, who, I venture to say, have administered the property in such a way as no other public trust has ever been administered in this country.

subtopic: VIRDEN, QTT'APPEDLE, REGINA AND MOOSEJAW TOWN SITES.
speechtext:
I do not know that

I can find fault with my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) for the tone In which he has discussed the report, a copy of which he has moved for. It might, perhaps, have been expected, under the circumstances, that my hon. friend would take an early opportunity of making a statement to the House which would explain, to some extent at least, the statements which were made in the report referred to. Some of the remarks my hon. friend has made would naturally leave a somewhat incorrect impression upon the minds of hon. members-though I desire to be understood as not in any way imputing that my hon. friend has intended to mislead the House. In the first place, so far as the refusal to furnish the Canadian Pacific Railway Company with the evidence upon which this report was made is concerned, I never heard of any such refusal until I heard it from my hon. friend just now. If the company had made application to me or had made application in such a way that it would have come before me personally-and I may say that the company has not shown any great backwardness in coming to my office and calling attention
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

subtopic: VIRDEN, QTT'APPEDLE, REGINA AND MOOSEJAW TOWN SITES.
speechtext: I may have been misunderstood as to the refusal. I have delayed asking this question, and the government have been applied to for a long time back, since shortly alter the report was made, and they have lulled to send the evidence. After the report was made, one would have thought that the evidence would be sent, but, up to this date, neither the Canadian Pacific Railway nor I have received nor been able to get the evidence.

subtopic: VIRDEN, QTT'APPEDLE, REGINA AND MOOSEJAW TOWN SITES.
speechtext:
What I was saying was this, that the government is not in the position of having refused to give a copy of any evidence taken by the commissioners; and I was proceeding to say that if the company wrote an ordinary official letter and did not receive it, they could have called my personal attention to it, and they would have received the papers without any delay whatever. So, there has been no intentional refusal to furnish any evidence or papers whatever. As to how this report came to be made- and as my hon. friend assumed a moderate tone in discussing the matter, I do not purpose going into the subject at length or making any strong remarks in regard to it, because the report will speak for itself when it is laid before the House-when I had been in office for some time, I experienced some difficulty in dealing with the accounts of the trust to which my hon. friend has referred; and, from time to time, it is necessary, for the purpose of carrying on the business of the department, to get more information than we were able to procure. At different times. I thought I would cause an examination of the accounts to be made for the purpose of getting an exact record of what had taken place. I may say that I Mr. SIFTON.
had not the least notion, in bringing about this examination, that my hon. friend or any of the trustees had been guilty of any personal dishonesty; but I thought-and I think now-that, as the minister responsible for the conduct of this business, it was my duty to direct an investigation into these accounts so that, as the minister responsible, I might know what had been done with the moneys, and also know in what manner the business had been conducted. The commission to make the examination was issued to two gentlemen both of whom are first-class accountants and both men thoroughly competent to conduct such an investigation, one being Mr. Smart, the Deputy Minister of the Interior, and the other Mr. E. F. Stephenson, who was an officer of the department before I took charge of it, and who is, I believe, a son of the late Rufus Stephenson, M.P. Mr. Stephenson is a most trusted officer of the department, one of the most competent in the service of the department. These two gentlemen went through the various accounts and made a thorough investigation and report. Now, the question whether the report is correct or not is a question which, if it is disputed, cannot be decided by an adverse statement made by Mr. Ogden, the' auditor of the Canadian Pacific Railway nor by a statement made by my hon. friend on the floor of this House. I have no intention of entering into an argument that the report of the commissioners was founded on fact. These gentlemen spent some time, I believe, in going through these accounts. It was a very laborious task, I was informed. The report speaks for itself. If its accuracy is disputed, that question can only be settled in the proper quarter by a judicial tribunal. The report having been made, we asked the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, who are responsible for the due performance of the trust, to place to our credit the amount of money which, the commissioners concluded, had been improperly charged against the government; and I think it is only necessary for me to state the facts to the House in order that the House may perceive that that was my plain duty under the circumstances, and that I could do neither more nor less. So far as the suggestion that my hon. friend has made that there was anything further than an effort to investigate this matter which had been made part of the business of the department and to have a proper record of it, and, when moneys were found to be due to the government to have them placed to our credit, I can only say there was nothing in my mind except simply to accomplish that purpose. And I submit, with all confidence that nothing further has been done. The question whether the moneys were properly charged against the government, whether the moneys found by the commissioners to be due to the government are to be paid or not is one which my hon. friend and I

cannot settle by debate in this House. I am free to say that I cannot agree with some things my hon. friend says. I cannot agree, for instance, in connection with the town site of Virden, that it was proper to charge the government one-half the cost of the town site when the government furnished half the land-I do not think they should be called upon to pay $3,200 for land they had furnished themselves. Then, to speak in connection with cases that seem very clear, I do not think that in the case of taxes paid by the trustees, all the taxes should have been charged against the government.
I am not going into a discussion of that, further than to say that the commissioners found that in the case of the taxes which were paid upon the property which the trustees held in trust, the government owning one-half of the land, the Canadian Pacific Railway one-quarter, and the Canada North-west Land Company one-quarter, the Canada North-west Land Company alone was liable for taxes. The trustees paid the taxes and they charged it up against the fund, so that the government had to pay its share of the taxes for which the Canada North-west Land Company was liable. The commissioners make a plain statement of the fact, and show that the money ought to be refunded. I have the report in my hand in which the commissioners state the facts. If there is any answer to that, it will be for the Canadian Pacific Railway, for my hon. friend and his co-trustees, to show it when the proper time comes. I have simply to say that upon the face of it, the report does not at all indicate that my hon. friend's statement is correct when he says there was nothing objectionable in regard to the transaction of the business by the trustees. When I say that, of course, my hon. friend and every member of the House will understand that I am not in the slightest degree suggesting there was anything improper from a personal standpoint, but only that close and personal supervision was not given by the trustees. In fact 1 presume my hon. friend had not an opportunity to give that personal supervision. Lord Strathcona, the High Commissioner, is equally responsible with him, and I do not suppose that Lord Strathcona ever saw or heard anything connected with it since the very early days of the trust.
But if my hon. friend thinks that there is anything in the slightest degree objectionable with regard to the position the department has taken, I can only say to him that the report having been made after full and careful investigation by gentlemen who were thoroughly competent for that purpose, and I am satisfied thoroughly unbiased in every possible way, I conceive it to be my duty to see that that money is collected and placed to the credit of the government. As for the government refusing
to agree to a division of the property concerned, I may say that I have never refused to make a division of the property. In fact for the last two years, I have desired that there should be such a division. My hon. friend will see that before we can have a division of the property we must have a settlement of the account, and the government are quite prepared that the account should be settled and the property divided as soon as possible. I have no desire to enter further into a discussion of the matter. A copy of the report will be duly laid upon the Table of the House, and hon. members will have an opportunity of judging of the statements for themselves.

subtopic: VIRDEN, QTT'APPEDLE, REGINA AND MOOSEJAW TOWN SITES.
speechtext:
The Minister of the Interior would have us believe that the government is always quite willing to refer this matter to the courts. Now, let me read him what Mr. Drinkwater says on the 9th of January:
1 have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 4th instant, informing me that the report of the commissioners who recently held an investigation in connection with the management of the town sites of Virden, Qu'Appelle, Regina and Moosejaw, a copy of which accompanied your letter, had been approved by order in council. I understand from these documents that the government proposes that the lands comprised in the town sites in question shall still he managed and dealt with by the present trustees, and in the manner indicated by that report, namely, that the sale of the lots shall be made to extend over a term of two or three years, in which time sales by public auction at intervals of certain of the lots could be held until the whole are disposed of. I am directed to say that this company prefers that the trusteeship be ended at once, and that a partition take place between the parties interested in these lands without delay. I shall be glad to know that this course is acceptable to the government, and that you are prepared to discuss the best method of carrying it into effect.
On behalf of the North-west Land Company that same request is made to the government. Then there Is another letter from Mr. Smart dealing with that question, and finally a letter on the 27th of February, referring to the question, pending the settlement of the accounts, In which he says :
X have yours of the 23rd instant, in reference to the division of the remaining lots in the towns of Virden, Qu'Appelle, Regina and Moose-jaw, and in reply would say that it Is not thought advisable to make a division at the present time. Will I return your maps to your address in Toronto?
There is a distinct refusal to make a division, no reference to a settlement. Now, then, with reference to the other matter of referring the question, the department say :
I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 7th instant, having reference to the report of the joint town site trustees, in which you intimate that the company would desire that the question a3 to placing to the credit of the

government the sums mentioned in the report as being due to the Crown should be submitted to the Exchequer Court, and requesting that a copy of the evidence taken by the commissioners may be forwarded to you on which to prepare the company's case, and you ask further whether the course suggested as to referring the matter to the Exchequer Court is agreeable to the government. In reply I am directed to say that the government has not decided upon any course with regard to this matter, except to ask the_company to make the necessary credits in the books of the trustees, so that the amount mentioned in the commissioner's report may be shown to be due to the government in this connection.
Now, it is plain as anything can be that the government refused to submit that matter to the Exchequer Court or to any court. They say that an amount of money arbitrarily found by partisan commissioners shall, without any reference, be at once acknowledged by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and by the trustees to be due to the government. That is directly and absolutely asked. In reference to the request that the matter be referred to the Exchequer Court, surely I am justified in saying the government refused to recognize that course. I think it is unreasonable, unfair, it is not the proper course to take under such circumstances. If the government found that the trustees were indebted to them and the trustees refused to acknowledge it, their only honourable course would have been to refer it at once to arbitration, or to some tribunal. These figures are arbitrary figures brought in by partisan auditors. On the other hand, the accounts sent in by the trustees from year to year have been approved by the government, the moneys have been paid to the government during all the twenty years they administered the trust, five years of which were under this government, to which they rendered statements in exactly the same manner as they rendered them under the late government. The trustees had no indication or suggestion from the government that everything was not absolutely right until this report was published in the Globe. That is the first that we ever heard of it.

speechtext: I think my hon. friend is trying to make a grievance where no grievance exists. The letter of Mr. Smart to which he refers is in regard to the question of submitting the matter to the Exchequer Court, and merely stating that the government had not decided finally upon a course. If the Canadian Pacific Railway secretary suggested a certain course, the government was not called upon immediately to assent to that, the government was entitled to give the matter consideration. The trustees have been handling this money and doing this business for many years.

speechtext: It is a matter of public business, it is not a matter of personal explanation. What I was about to say was that my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) is endeavouring to make a mountain out of a molehill. He has endeavoured to show that we have refused to refer this to the courts, because Mr. Smart simply said that the government had not decided upon that course. In so far as the other question is concerned, to which Mr. Smart's other letter referred, the letter is simply one of a similar character. It does not make a final decision, nor does it profess to do so. I think my hon. friend will find, when he comes to go into this matter with the same degree of care that the commissioners have gone into it, that his ideas upon the subject will undergo somewhat of a change, and I think he will find that the statement he has made, that this is the report of partisan auditors, is not justified by the fact. If the word ' partisan ' is used in the sense in which it refers to the political proclivities of the commissioners, certainly, Mr. E. F. Stephenson could not be considered to be a partisan of this government, and I think, therefore, that the personnel of the commission was as fair and as free from partisan bias as it could possibly be under the circumsances.
